        • np 3 - tatiyakaṭhinasikkhāpada
          • background #editing
          • description #editing
            • When a bhikkhu’s robe has been done or kaṭhina privileges have been removed, if a bhikkhu receives an out-of-season robe he can accept it, if he prefers. Once accepted he must quickly make it a robe (according to NP1). If the cloth received is not enough to be made into a robe and if it is expected that extra cloth will be received from some other source to fulfil the need, the first cloth can be kept for up to one month. Even while expecting extra cloth, if the first cloth is kept for more than a month, it will be nissaggiya. A pācittiya offence will also be committed.
          • counting days
            • if the cloth is an akālacīvara, one wishes to make a robe but it is not enough for making the desired robe, and the monk expects more cloth, it (the mūlacīvara) can be kept for up to {{3162409382145037::30 days}} if the paccāsācīvara (expected cloth) is received on any day until the 20th day, the paccāsacīvara changes the mūlacīvara into its own category (attano gatikaṁ karoti) making both last for {{3162409382145037::10 days}}; e.g.: if paccāsācīvara is received on the 5th day ⇒ both mūla and paccāsa cīvaras last {{3162409382145037::10 more days}} if the paccāsācīvara is received after the 20th day, the mūlacīvara changes the paccāsacīvara into its own category (attano gatikaṁ karoti) making both last up to the {{3162409382145037::30th day}}; e.g.: if paccāsācīvara is received on the 25th day ⇒ both mūla and paccāsa cīvaras last {{3162409382145037::5 more days}} if the paccāsācīvara is not received before the dawn of the {{3162409382145037::31st day}}, the mūlacīvara, if neither done vikappana, nor adhiṭṭhāna nor given away, becomes nissaggiya and the monk incurs a pācittiya offense (evaṃ pana avatvā yasmā antarā uppajjamāne paccāsācīvare mūlacīvarassa uppannadivasato yāva vīsatimo divaso tāva uppannaṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ mūlacīvaraṃ attano gatikaṃ karoti, tato uddhaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ attano gatikaṃ karoti.)
          • pāḷi terms
            • cīvaramāsa↔the "robe-month" which is the last month of the rainy season when the kaṭhina is spread (Kattika month)
            • akālasamaya↔the period outside the cīvarakālasamaya; it can be the whole year if one has not observed vassa, broken it or observed pacchimikā vassa; if one has not spread the kaṭhina it lasts for 11 months apart from the ordinary cīvarakālasamaya; if the kaṭhina was spread, it lasts for 7 months apart from the 5 months of cīvarakālasamaya
            • akālacīvara↔an "out-of-season robe" which is a cloth received outside the cīvarakālasamaya (Buddha uses the word cīvara to refer to such cloth), or a cloth received during the kālasamaya but specified by the donor as such
            • mūlacīvara↔the first cloth received, which is not enough for making the desired robe
            • paccāsācīvara↔the expected cloth, which fulfils the need for more cloth for making the desired robe
          • the kaṭhina is spread during which period?→during the last month of the rainy season (the Kattika month, the ordinary cīvarakālasamaya; the cīvaramāsa)
          • what is the purpose of this rule?→it is to relax the paṭhamakaṭhinasikkhāpada giving the monk more time to find the necessary cloth for making a robe
          • aṅga (factors)
            • ...ubbhatasmiṁ kaṭhine...: having no kaṭhinānisaṁsa
            • ...akālacīvaraṁ uppajjeyya...:
              • ...paṭiggahetabbaṁ...: a cloth that belongs to oneself
              • the cloth being vikappanūpaga
              • being an atirekacīvara
            • māsaparamaṁ...: the elapse of 30 days from the day it was received
            • important note:
              • ...khippameva kāretabbaṁ...: even though not mentioned, the monk must have the intention to make a robe
              • ...no cassa pāripūri satiyā paccāsāya...: the cloth must not be enough to make such robe and the monk must have the expectation of receiving extra cloth for making such robe
          • nissajjana (not for exam)
            • in the presence of the Saṅgha {{3314794728246877::idaṃ me, bhante, akālacīvaraṃ māsātikkantaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ }}{{3314794728246877::saṅghassa}}{{3314794728246877:: nissajjāmi.}} in the presence of 2 or 3 bhikkhus {{3314794728246877::idaṃ me, bhante, akālacīvaraṃ māsātikkantaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ }}{{3314794728246877::āyasmantānaṃ}}{{3314794728246877:: nissajjāmi.}} in the presence of a single bhikkhu {{3314794728246877::idaṃ me, bhante, akālacīvaraṃ māsātikkantaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ }}{{3314794728246877::āyasmato}}{{3314794728246877:: nissajjāmi.}}
        • np 4 - purāṇacīvarasikkhāpada
          • background
            • the Tathāgata was residing in the Jetavana, Sāvatthi at one time; Ven. Udāyī's ex-wife went forth among the bhikkhunis and they would frequently visit each other; one day, he sat on a seat in front of her exposing his genitals and she also did the same; while looking at her genitals lustfully, he emitted semen; then the inner robe was taken by her to wash, and she took some of the semen in her mouth. A portion of it was inserted into her genitals. This made her pregnant. Following this particular incident, the Buddha declared a training rule prohibiting monks from getting their robes washed by unrelated bhikkhunis
            • notes:
              • the bhikkhunis end up having to be protected by the monks which increases their association
              • the bhikkhunis are encouraged to associate monks and the monks protect the bhikkhunis, but at the same time bhikkhunis are agocara for bhikkhus
              • 2 rules to control the distance between unrelated monks and nuns
              • the rules only refers to bhikkhunis, that is maybe because of the difference in sīla which naturally distances bhikkhus from the other non-bhikkhunis (the anupasampannas might also be more under watch which naturally distances them from the bhikkhus)
              • payanti (breastfeeding) bhikkhuni: she can take care of the child but after some period the child has to be given to someone's custody
              • one is naturally not attracted to a relative and an unrelated one does not know the limits, therefore the limitations were imposed on unrelated ones
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • yo pana bhikkhu aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā purāṇacīvaraṃ dhovāpeyya vā rajāpeyya vā ākoṭāpeyya vā, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ (If a monk gets an unrelated female monk to wash, die or beat a used robe a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will be committed)
            • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • purāṇa [pura + aṇa]↔adj. previous; old; ancient; 2 adj. worn out; old; used
              • ākoṭāpeti [ā + √kuṭ + *āpe + ti]↔pr. (+acc) makes beat; causes to pound; makes pummel
          • description
            • what is the purpose of this training rule?→to avoid bhikkhus from getting their robes washed by unrelated bhikkhunis since the brahmacariya could be adversely impacted by innapropriate relationships with unrelated bhikkhunis
          • pāḷi terms
            • ñātaka
              • ñātaka
                • blood relations 7 generations up and down from one's parents, including all siblings and their children, never going beyond the 7th generation; in-laws are not included
                • (-7) 6th great grandparents
                • (-6) 5th great grandparents
                • (-5) 4th great grandparents
                • (-4) 3rd great grandparents
                • (-3) 2nd great grandparents
                • (-2) great grandparents
                • (-1) grandparents
                • (0) mother & father
                • (1) ahaṁ
                • (2) my son
                • (3) grandson
                • (4) great grandson
                • (5) 2nd great grandson
                • (6) 3rd great grandson
                • (7) 4th great grandson
                • note: 6th great grandparents could be called 7th grandparents; 4th great grandson could be called 5th grandson
              • dasa ñātakā (pāḷi for exam)
                • mother - mātā
                • father - pitā
                • mother's younger sister (aunt) - cūḷamātā or mātucchā
                • mother's elder sister (aunt) - mahāmātā or mātucchā
                • father's sister (aunt) - pitucchā
                • father's younger brother (uncle) - cūḷapitā
                • father's elder brother (uncle) - mahāpitā
                • mother's brother (uncle) - mātula
                • daughter - dhītā
                • son - putta
                • mem aid:
                  • women first
                    • parents
                    • their siblings
                    • children
              • note:
                • buddha addressed the relatives by their names; in some places in the canon tāta is used
                • it should be noted that in-laws are not considered relatives under this context
            • bhikkhuni
              • 4 types of bhikkhunis
                • aṭṭhagarudhammehi upasampannā: this is Mahā Pajāpatī Gotamī, the younger sister of the Buddha’s mother (who was also his stepmother), who received the higher ordination by accepting the eight cardinal rules made by the Buddha
                • ekato (paripuṇṇa) upasampannā: nuns ordained following Mahāpajāpatī gotamī (500) until aṭṭhavācikupasampadā was established and bhikkhus who went through a natural sex change (only one case recorded)
                • ekato (aparipuṇṇa) upasampannā: after aṭṭhavācikupasampadā was established, nuns who had been ordained by the bhikkhunī saṅgha but not yet from the bhikkhu saṅgha were so called; they are not a full-fledged bhikkhunī
                • ubhato upasampannā: a bhikkhuni ordained by both saṅghas
                • note: the aparipuṇṇa is not included under the term bhikkhuni in bhikkhu rules; offenses regarding aparipuṇṇas are lighter
            • purāṇacīvara (used robe)
              • a nivāsana parūpana robe that is dyed and marked (kappabindu) that was used at least once for wearing or covering, making contact with the body (kāyaparibhoga)
              • note:
                • it includes kāyaparibhoga such as carrying it on the shoulder, on the head, using it as a pillow, etc
                • it does not include using it without coming into contact with it, such as using it as a shade (holding it over one's head) or as a sheet under the paccattharaṇa
            • nivāsana robe↔robe that is worn on the body as antaravāsaka
            • pārupana robe↔robe that is worn on the body as uttarāsaṅga
            • kāyaparibhoga↔using with the body, including lying / sitting on it, putting it on the head, etc
          • instances of offenses
            • ordering, verbally or bodily, the purāṇacīvara to be washed / dyed / beaten by an unrelated bhikkhunī: {{4881002354953168::dkṭ for each command}} she then does as was ordered: {{4881002354953168::np for the first function, dkṭ for each extra function}} she does more functions than was ordered: {{4881002354953168::anāpatti}} giving it on her hands, leaving it at her feet, throwing it up or sending it via a sikkhāmāna, sāmaṇera, sāmaṇerī, lay devotee or titthiya from a distance of up to {{4881002354953168::12 hattha}}, and she then washes / dyes / beats it: {{4881002354953168::np}} preceding actions done by the unrelated bhikkhunī before the robe is washed / the dying process complete / the first beat: {{4881002354953168::each preceding action is a dkṭ for the monk}} in the case of washing, when is the np committed? {{4881002354953168::the moment the washed robe is lifted}} in the case of dying, when is the np committed? {{4881002354953168::the moment the dying is complete}} in the case of beating, when is np committed? {{4881002354953168::the moment it is first beaten}} regardless to whom it was given (sikkhamānā, sāmaṇerī, upāsikā, or even a bhikkhu, sāmaṇera or upāsaka who then undergoes sex change), if it ends up being washed by such person as an unrelated bhikkhunī: {{4881002354953168::np}} if the monk says, “You must know the related functions of this robe or perform them”, etc, and she does all 3 functions of washing / dyeing / beating: {{4881002354953168::1 dkṭ for commanding, 1 pc, 2 dkṭ and the robe becomes nissaggiya}} if the monk is not aware the robe is a purāṇacīvara or that the bhikkhunī is not related: {{4881002354953168::np (this rule is acittaka and asaññāvimokkha)}} lustfully looking at a vagina: {{4881002354953168::dkṭ}} these also apply for the np17 (eḷakalomadhovāpana)
            • the pācittiya does not substitute the dkṭs? no, this is under samanubhāsanakamma
          • aṅgāni
            • aññātikāya bhikkhunīya: ordering an aññātika bhikkhuni, who is within the proximity of 12 cubits, to wash, dye or beat the robe
            • purāṇacīvaraṁ: the robe being a purāṇa cīvara
            • dhovāpeyya vā rajāpeyya vā ākoṭāpeyya vā: that same bhikkhuni carrying one of the ordered activities such as washing, dying or beating
          • nissajjana
            • “Idaṃ me, bhante, puraṇacīvaraṃ aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā dhovāpitaṃ (rajāpitaṃ / ākoṭāpitaṃ) nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.”
          • questions
            • a bhikkhu orders an unrelated bhikkhuni, “Sister, you should perform all the work related to this robe”, and hands it over to her; she washes, dyes, and beats the robe; what are the offences the monk committed?→dkṭ for ordering, pc, dkṭ, and dkṭ, (and the robe becomes nissaggiya)
        • np 5 - cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing in the Veḷuvana monastery in the city of Rājagaha. One day, Bhikkhuni Uppalavanna meditated after her meal at the forest called Andhavana. A group of thieves also came into the area with stolen goods. The head of the group saw the bhikkhuni in advance, and he changed their route thinking that his group of thieves would hurt her. Further, a part of the meat that was cooked for him was wrapped up and hung on a tree close to the bhikkhuni saying “May whoever sees it take it.” The bhikkhuni picked up the parcel of meat and went to the Veḷuvanārāma. She gave the meat to Udāyī Thera to be offered to the Buddha, and in this instance Venerable Udāyī requested for her antarāvāsaka (inner robe). She had to hand it over to him unwillingly. The Buddha, being aware of this, declared the training rule, prohibiting monks from accepting robes from nuns. After this rule was established, bhikkhus did not accept robes from bhikkhunis, even in exchange for something. Knowing this, the Buddha later added an amendment allowing monks to accept robes from bhikkhunis as an exchange for something else.
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Yo pana bhikkhu aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā hatthato cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇheyya aññatra pārivaṭṭakā nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. (If a monk accepts robes from an unrelated bhikkhuni except as an exchange for something else, a pācittiya offence will be committed.)
          • description
            • purpose of the rule→to prevent possible unnecessary relationships between bhikkhus and unrelated bhikkhunis
          • pāḷi terms
            • cīvara under this rule refers to→a vikappanūpaga robe (any cloth of allowable material for robes of a minimum dimension of 4 x 8 sugataṅguli); it includes a vassāvāsika robe
            • pārivaṭṭaka (m.) [pari + √vaṭṭ + *aka]↔exchange; swap; trade; lit. turning around
              • the monk must give in exchange for the robe at least {{10155562418222086::an āmalaka fruit}}; the exchange does not need be at the same time; as long as the monk has the intention of giving something in exchange it is ok
            • 3 ways in which the robe may be accepted under this rule
              • from hand to hand (direct acceptance)
              • from hand to feet, if the bhikkhu accepts it mentally
                • note: if taken with paṁsukūlasañña it is allowable
              • by throwing from any distance, even beyond 12 hattha, if the bhikkhu accepts it mentally
              • note: if the robe is sent via an {{434447424982904::anupasampanna }}it is allowable, but via an {{434447424982904::upasampanna}} it entails the full offense
            • 2 ways of accepting the robe as an exchange
              • accepting it while giving something in exchange for it
              • accepting it with the intention of giving something in exchange for it later
          • instances of offenses
            • accepting a vikappanūpaga robe from an unrelated bhikkhunī without giving anything in return: {{12877093398209172::np}} if the bhikkhunī leaves it at the monk's feet and the monk mentally accepts it: {{12877093398209172::np}} if a bhikkhunī, within the range of 12 hattha, throws the robe and the monk accepts it mentally: {{12877093398209172::np}} if a bhikkhunī, even beyond the range of 12 hattha, throws the robe and the monk accepts it mentally: {{12877093398209172::np}} if the bhikkhunī sends the robe via an anupasampanna and the monk accepts it: {{12877093398209172::no offense}} if it is offered via another upasampanna: {{12877093398209172::np}} if the bhikkhunī leaves the robe on the ground thinking, "may a monk take this as paṁsukūla", and a monk takes it as paṁsukūla: {{12877093398209172::no offense}} and if the monk takes it thinking, "this robe has been kept for me": {{12877093398209172::np }}{{12877093398209172::(Kaṅ-abh-ṭ. 304: Paṃsukūlaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvāti “Assāmikaṃ ida”nti saññaṃ uppādetvā. Assāmikañhi “Paṃsukūla”nti vuccati. Iminā “Amhākamatthāya ṭhapita”ntiādikāya saññāya gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti)}} when the monk extends his arm to accept the robe without intending to give something in exchange: {{12877093398209172::dkṭ}} and when he accepts it: {{12877093398209172::np}} if she offers the robe to the saṅgha: {{12877093398209172::no offense}}
          • aṅgāni
            • aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā...paṭiggaṇheyya: receiving the robe from an aññātika bhikkhuni
            • cīvaraṁ: the robe being vikappanūpaga
            • aññatra pārivaṭṭakā: being a robe that has not been accepted in exchange for something
          • nissajjana
            • “Idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā hatthato paṭiggahitaṃ, aññatra pārivattakā nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.”
          • questions
            • who were the two characters involved in the story which led to the first promulgation (mūla paññatti) of the cīvarapaṭiggahaṇa nissaggiya training rule?→upalavaṇṇattherī and udāyitthera
        • np 6 - aññātakaviññattisikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Jetavana temple near Sāvatthi. Venerable Upananda who was a son of the Sākyan clan is an eloquent Dhamma orator. One rich person (seṭṭhi) who was impressed by his sermons, requested that he be informed if the priest requires any of the requisites. Then, Upananda Thera, requested one of the shawls out of the two he was wearing. Since the rich man could not offer one of them and return home in one shawl, he promised that he would send the shawl after having reached home. Venerable Upananda did not agree to this idea and insisted that the shawl be given immediately. Then, the rich man gave one of his shawls and went home with one shawl. The people who got to know about this incident began to bad-mouth the priest. Therefore, this training rule was declared inhibiting monks from asking for robes from unrelated lay devotees. On another occasion, robes of bhikkhus who had embarked on a long journey were stolen. Since the Buddha had laid down a training rule prohibiting monks from asking for robes from aññātika and appavārita lay devotees, the monks whose robes were looted came back to the Buddha naked. They even paid respect to the Buddha unclothed. Thus, based on this instance, a sub charter was declared for this training rule
            • who is the venerable usually connected with the rules regarding robes?→Upananda Thera
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Yo pana bhikkhu aññātakaṃ gahapatiṃ vā gahapatāniṃ vā cīvaraṃ viññāpeyya, aññatra samayā, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ samayo, acchinnacīvaro vā hoti bhikkhu naṭṭhacīvaro vā ayaṃ tattha samayo. (A monk asks for a robe from an unrelated male or female householder during an inappropriate time (and obtains it). For this act the monk commits a nissaggiya pācittiya offence. What is the suitable time to ask for robes? When the robes have been stolen by thieves or when the robes have been destroyed. These are the suitable occasions to ask for robes from lay devotees.)
            • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • viññāpeti [vi + √ñā + *āpe + ti] or [na > a + √chid + na]↔pr. (+acc) makes intelligible; lit. causes to know; 2 pr. (+acc) asks (for); requests; begs (for); 3 pr. (+acc) makes known (to); informs; communicates (to)
              • acchinna↔pp. (+instr) robbed (by); stolen (by); snatched (by); pinched (by) [ā + √chid + na]; 2.1 pp. not cut off [na > a + √chid + na]; 2.2 pp. new, not yet cut up (of cloth); 2.3 pp. unbroken; not interrupted; consistent [na > a + √chid + na]
              • naṭṭha [√nas + ta]↔pp. lost; perished; destroyed
          • description
            • what is the purpose of this rule?→to prevent monks from making unsuitable requests from a aññātaka appavārita dāyaka
          • pāḷi terms
            • pavārita↔a lay devotee who has invited a monk to request for things within the limits of the invitation (under this rule it must be an invitation with regard to any requisites or at least with regard to robes) note: the donor is not bound to give after inviting; if the donor changes or rescinds the invitation, the donor becomes one who has not invited
            • appavārita dāyaka under this rule is→a lay devotee who has not invited a monk with regard to any requisites or at least with regard to robes
            • acchinnacīvaro samayo↔the occasion in which at least 2 robes have been stolen
            • naṭṭhacīvaro samayo↔the occasion in which at least 2 robes (starting with 3) have been destroyed or decayed beyond a usable state
          • asking and exchanging
            • ñātaka one can ask for: {{9661939282173797::anything}} can one exchange things with them?: {{9661939282173797::no}} sahadhammika asking: {{9661939282173797::anything}} exchanging: {{9661939282173797::yes}} pavārita gihī asking: {{9661939282173797::according to invitation}} exchange: {{9661939282173797::no}} appavārita gihī: asking: {{9661939282173797::no}} exchanging: {{9661939282173797::no}}
          • samaya
            • in which occasions robes can be requested from an aññātaka appavārita gihī?→when at least 2 of them have been stolen (acchinnacīvaro), destroyed or decayed beyond their usable state (naṭṭhacīvaro), or lost
              • in which of the 2 samayas is lost included in? #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • instance of offences
            • asking from aññātaka appavārita gihī during an inappropriate time: {{6029561509286445::dkṭ}} accepting the robe: {{6029561509286445::np}} doing so while mistakenly perceiving the gihī as ñātaka or pavārita: {{6029561509286445::np}} doing so while mistakenly perceiving the time to be appropriate: {{6029561509286445::np}}
          • aṅgāni
            • aññātakaṁ gahapatiṁ ... viññāpeyya: requesting a robe from a aññātaka and appavārita lay sponsor
            • cīvaraṁ: being a vikappanūpaga robe
            • samaya: inappropriate time period to request for robes
            • result: receiving the robe
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ aññātakaṃ gahapatikaṃ, aññatra samayā viññāpitaṃ, nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.
          • note:
            • duration of the invitation: some monks consider that if the time is not mentioned by the donor it is only for 4 months, but in Galduwa it is considered as without time limit
            • sanghika and puggalika pavāraṇas are different
        • np 7 - tatuttarisikkhāpada
          • background
            • Once the Buddha was residing in the Jetavana monastery near Sāvatthi. Chabbaggiya monks approached the monks whose robes were lost or destroyed and said: “Friends, the Tathāgata has allowed monks whose robes are lost or destroyed to ask for robes from unrelated and appavārita devotees. Therefore, you ask for robes from aññātaka and appavārita devotees. If not we shall ask on behalf of you.” Then they went to such householders and requested for robes. Later the monks whose robes were lost or destroyed also went to those householders and requested for the same. Upon being requested, most of the householders said that they had already given robes for monks whose robes were lost or destroyed. Further, they accused monks for asking for robes abundantly. Hearing this news, the Buddha promulgated the following training rule.
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • tañce aññātako gahapati vā gahapatānī vā bahūhi cīvarehi abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya santaruttaraparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā tato cīvaraṃ sāditabbaṃ, tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. (When an unrelated devotee is offering a monk with many robes (upon a request made by the monk due to his robes being destroyed or lost), he should only accept two robes that are sufficient to be used as his under robe and upper robe. Should the monk accept more than that, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will be committed.)
            • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • abhihaṭṭhuṃ inf. [abhi + √har + tuṃ]↔(+acc) to take away ; 2 to bring over
              • sādiyati [√sād + *e + iya + ti]↔pr. (+acc) consents (to); accepts; agrees (to); permits; lit. causes to be tasted
          • description
            • purpose of the rule→to prevent monks from taking more than what is needed to cover themselves in such situations where the monk has asked an aññātaka appavārita gihī for robes
          • amount of robes that can be taken
            • in brief: after asking, the monk or nun should not have more than {{31696790231102945::2 robes}} in detail: bhikkhu starting with 3 robes missing 3, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}} missing 2, can take: {{31696790231102945::1}} missing 1, can take: {{31696790231102945::0 (cannot ask)}} starting with 2 robes missing 2, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}} missing 1, can take: {{31696790231102945::1}} starting with 1 robe missing 1, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}} bhikkhuni starting with 5 robes missing 5, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}} missing 4, can take: {{31696790231102945::1}} missing 3 or less, can take: {{31696790231102945::0 (cannot ask)}} starting with 4 robes missing 4, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}} missing 3, can take: {{31696790231102945::1}} missing 2 or less, can take: {{31696790231102945::0 (cannot ask)}} starting with 3 robes: missing 3, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}} missing 2, can take: {{31696790231102945::1}} missing 1, can take: {{31696790231102945::0 (cannot ask)}} starting with 2 robes: missing 2, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}} missing 1, can take: {{31696790231102945::1}} starting with 1 robe: missing 1, can take: {{31696790231102945::2}}
          • aṅgāni
            • aññātako gahapati: requesting from a aññātaka appavārita devotee
            • santaruttaraparamaṁ: requesting more than what is required to cover oneself
            • sādiyeyya: receiving them
            • samaya: robes have been lost, stolen, destroyed, etc
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ aññātakaṃ gahapatikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tatuttari viññāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.
          • note:
            • bhikkhunīs have 5 robes
            • it is not mentioned whether it is a made robe or just a cloth
            • if the robe is given away, it is not mentioned whether one can ask or not, but it may be allowed (mgvhr)
        • np 8 - paṭhamaupakkhaṭasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing in the Jetavana, Sāvatthi. One man says as follows to his wife: “How do I offer a robe to Upananda Thera?”. Upananda Thera, who came to know about these words, approached the man and inquired: “You have been looking to offer me a robe. Is that true?” He had further said that, if so, offer me this particular robe. Then the man had started bad- mouthing the priest and scolding him. Bhikkhus who became aware of this situation, informed this to the Tathāgata. At this instance, the Tathāgata declared the following training rule.
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Bhikkhuṃ paneva uddissa aññātakassa gahapatissa vā gahapatāniyā vā cīvaracetāpannaṃ upakkhaṭaṃ hoti “iminā cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ cīvarena acchādessāmī”ti, tatra ce so bhikkhu pubbe appavārito upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjeyya, “sādhu vata maṃ āyasmā iminā cīvaracetāpannena evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā acchādehī” ti, kalyāṇakamyataṃ upādāya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. (If an unrelated householder or housewife sets up a robe fund for the monks with the intention of purchasing a robe for a particular monk from it, and if the monk who has not previously been invited to mention his needs for robes instructs as follows: “Devotee, please purchase a robe with such and such qualities and give it to me” and make known his likings and desires, and if he commands for a robe more valuable than the money set aside and receives it, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will be committed)
            • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • cetāpanna (nt.) [√cit + *āpe + ana]↔fund; account; lit. exchanging; bartering
              • upakkhaṭa [upa + √kar + ta]↔pp. prepared; set-up; supplied; arranged 2 adj. brought near
              • itthaṃ (ind.) [ima + tha + aṃ]↔thus; such; in this way
              • acchādeti [ā + √chad + *e + ti]↔pr. (+acc) dresses; clothes; give clothes (to); lit. covers
              • vikappa (m.)[vi + √kapp + a]↔(+loc) alteration (to); improvement (to); distinction (regarding); lit. more suitable
              • kalyāṇakamyatā (f.) [kalyāṇa + kamyatā]↔desire for something good; wanting something of quality
          • description
            • in which circumstance a monk is allowed to tell a dāyaka to offer a robe under this rule? what are the limits of such request?→it is allowed if the dāyaka has set aside a sum of money for that purpose, because the money has already been allocated to the bhikkhu; the bhikkhu may ask for a robe or requisite of equal or lower value in comparison to the funds set aside
          • instances of offences
            • if a monk requests a robe that is more valuable than the robe-fund: {{17063493168012633::dkṭ}} if the monk accepts the robe: {{17063493168012633::np}} if he requests for something of the same value: {{17063493168012633::anāpatti}} if he requests for something of less value: {{17063493168012633::anāpatti}}
          • aṅgāni
            • aññātakassa gahapatissa...appavārito: the lay sponsor of concern being aññātaka and appavārita
            • cīvare vikappaṁ āpajjeyya...evarūpaṁ...acchādehi: asking for a more valuable robe than the robe-fund
            • receiving the robe
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ pubbe appavārito aññātakaṃ gahapatikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṃ āpannaṃ nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi
          • note:
            • a living buddha's body marks, rays, life, and 4 requisites (before offered) cannot be destroyed or stolen
              • kassapa buddha's monastery was destroyed
        • np 9 - dutiyaupakkhaṭasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing in the Jetavana, Sāvatthi. The only difference in this trainingrule is that two or more people are approached for the same command as the paṭhamaupakkhaṭa
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Bhikkhuṃ paneva uddissa ubhinnaṃ aññātakānaṃ gahapatīnaṃ vā gahapatānīnaṃ vā paccekacīvaracetāpannāni upakkhaṭāni honti, “imehi mayaṃ paccekacīvaracetāpannehi paccekacīvarāni cetāpetvā itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ cīvarehi acchādessāmā” ti, tatra ce so bhikkhu pubbe appavārito upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjeyya, “sādhu vata maṃ āyasmanto imehi paccekacīvaracetāpannehi evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā acchādetha, ubhova santā ekenā” ti, kalyāṇakamyataṃ upādāya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. (If two unrelated householders or two housewives build up two robe funds for the monks, with the intention of purchasing separate robes for a particular monk from them, and if the monk who has not previously been invited to mention his needs for robes instructs as follows: “Devotees, please get together and purchase a robe with such and such qualities from both robe funds and offer it to me” and make known his likings and desires, and if he commands for a robe more valuable than the money set aside and receives it, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will be committed.)
            • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • ubhinnaṃ↔to both; for both
              • pacceka [pati + eka]↔adj. individual; separate; each
              • paccekacīvara (nt.)↔individual robe; separate robe
          • aṅgāni
            • ubhinnaṁ aññātakānaṁ gahapatīnaṁ: the lay sponsors of concern being aññātaka and appavārita
            • vikappaṁ āpajjeyya...paccekacīvaracetāpannehi...: asking that a robe that is more in value than the collective robe-fund be bought
            • receiving the robe
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ pubbe appavārito aññātake gahapatike upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṃ āpannaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.
          • note:
            • what is the relationship between the paṭhama and the dutiyaupakkaṭa sikkhāpadas?→the only differences are that the second is with regard to two or more donors, and is like an anupaññatti of the first one
        • np 10 - rājasikkhāpada
          • background
            • Buddha in: Jetavana, Sāvatthi monk in question: Upanandatthera gist: one of Upanandatthera’s attendant ministers sent robe-fund (cīvaracetāpanna) via a messenger; he rejected it, and it was handed over to a helper; the minister sent several messages via a messenger stating that he would like to see the priest get a robe prepared with his money and wear it; the thera visited the helper at his house and informed his need for a robe; it happened to be that there was a meeting of the residents of that trade village on this day and if one were to arrive late, a fine of fifty coins would have to be paid; therefore, the helper pleaded the thera to wait for a day but he insisted, so a robe was brought and given to him; the helper arrived late at the meeting and had to pay the fine; the villagers then criticized the monks leading to the laying down of this rule
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Bhikkhuṃ paneva uddissa rājā vā rājabhoggo vā brāhmaṇo vā gahapatiko vā dūtena cīvaracetāpannaṃ pahiṇeyya, ‘iminā cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ cīvarena acchādehī’ti. So ce dūto taṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya, ‘Idaṃ kho, bhante, āyasmantaṃ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṃ ābhataṃ, paṭiggaṇhātu āyasmā cīvaracetāpanna’nti, tena bhikkhunā so dūto evamassa vacanīyo, ‘Na kho mayaṃ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma, cīvarañca kho mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma, kālena kappiya’nti. So ce dūto taṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ vadeyya, ‘Atthi panāyasmato koci veyyāvaccakaro’ti. Cīvaratthikena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā veyyāvaccakaro niddisitabbo ārāmiko vā upāsako vā, ‘Eso kho, āvuso, bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro’ti. So ce dūto taṃ veyyāvaccakaraṃ saññāpetvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya ‘Yaṃ kho bhante, āyasmā (nom.) veyyāvaccakaraṃ niddisi saññatto so mayā, upasaṅkamatu āyasmā kālena, cīvarena taṃ acchādessatī’ti, cīvaratthikena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā veyyāvaccakaro upasaṅkamitvā dvattikkhattuṃ codetabbo sāretabbo, ‘Attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā’ti. Dvattikkhattuṃ codayamāno sārayamāno taṃ cīvaraṃ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, no ce abhinipphādeyya, catukkhattuṃ pañcakkhattuṃ chakkhattuparamaṃ tuṇhībhūtena uddissa ṭhātabbaṃ. Catukkhattuṃ pañcakkhattuṃ chakkhattuparamaṃ tuṇhībhūto uddissa tiṭṭhamāno taṃ cīvaraṃ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; tato ce uttari vāyamamāno taṃ cīvaraṁ abhinipphādeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. No ce abhinipphādeyya, yatassa cīvaracetāpannaṃ ābhataṃ, tattha sāmaṃ vā gantabbaṃ dūto vā pāhetabbo ‘Yaṃ kho tumhe āyasmanto bhikkhuṃ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṃ pahiṇittha, na taṃ tassa bhikkhuno kiñci atthaṃ anubhoti, yuñjantāyasmanto sakaṃ, mā vo sakaṃ vinassā’ti, ayaṃ tattha sāmīci. If a king, minister, brahmin or householder gives money to a messenger in the interest of a particular monk and orders: “Please use this money to purchase a robe and offer the robe to the monk”; and if the messenger goes up to the particular monk and says: “This money has been brought for you. May you accept this money given for a robe”, the monk must say as follows: “Friend, we cannot accept these funds. When the suitable time comes, an appropriate robe will be accepted.” Then the messenger asks the monk: “Do you have an attendant?” At that time, the monk may point out a lay resident of the monastery or a lay devotee saying “This is our attendant.” Then the messenger consults the attendant and approaches the monk and says: “I have informed the attendant pointed by you. He will purchase a robe when a suitable time arrives.” Then, monks, the monk who is in need of robes should tell the attendant that he requires robes. This can be done two or three times. If the robe is obtained after (one), two or three reminders, it is fine. If still not received, the monk can approach the attendant and stand in front of him silently as a reminding gesture. If the robe is obtained by this approach of four to six silent-standings, it is fine. If further effort is directed beyond this point to get the robe, and it is actually obtained, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will transpire
            • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • rājabhogga [rāja + bhogga]↔adj. suitable to be used by a king; useful to a king; 2 (m.) king’s minister; royal official; lit. wealth of a king

              • sāmīci (f.)↔right way; correct course; proper procedure
          • description
            • what is the purpose behing this rule?
              • to establish the code of conduct for monks when money is offered and when money is kept with a kappiya for the sake of robes
            • what happens if the monk points to the attendant without having been asked for it? #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • pāḷi terms
            • vāra↔the times / attempts / prompts a monk can do to a fund-keeper in order to get a robe
              • how can the monk prompt the kappiya? (vāra)
                • a monk can prompt the fund-keeper for a maximum of 12 vāra: verbally reminding one's needs equals to 2 vāra; standing in silence in his presence is 1 vāra possibilities: 6 verbal prompts 5 verbal prompts and 2 silent stands 4 verbal prompts and 4 silent stands 3 verbal prompts and 6 silent stands 2 verbal prompts and 8 silent stands 1 verbal prompt and 10 silent stands 12 silent stands
          • instances of offenses
            • a monk is offered money, how should he proceed?→he must simply reject it saying, "na kho mayaṁ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṁ paṭiggaṇhāma, cīvarañca kho mayaṁ paṭiggaṇhāma kālena kappiyaṁ", and he must not point to a kappiya nor tell the donor to give the money to the kappiya
            • when can a kappiya be shown?→only if the donor asks if the monk has a kappiya can the monk show it but the monk must not tell the donor to give the money to the kappiya
            • under which conditions can the monk inform the kappiya his needs?→only if the donor leaves the money with the kappiya and either the donor or the kappiya informs the monk inviting him to ask for his needs, otherwise the monk cannot ask
            • what is the proper way of asking for a robe?→ it should be done by saying "attho me āvuso cīvarena" (I'm in need of a robe, friend), the monk must not say, "civaraṁ me dehi" (give me a robe)
            • if while the monk is standing in silence the kappiya asks him what is his purpose how should the monk behave?→the monk is allowed to say "You know the purpose"; if the monk says more than that such as, "I'm in need of a robe", it counts as a verbal prompt, not as a silent stand
            • a monk receives a robe from the fund-keeper after having prompted him more than 12 vāra: {{39142474742036826::np}} if a monk receives a robe mistakenly thinking the 12 vāras have not been exceeded when they actually have: {{39142474742036826::np}} if the 12 vāra are used up and the robe was not produced the original donor should be informed, otherwise: {{39142474742036826::dkṭ}}
          • this sikkhāpada is (sacittaka / acittaka) {{14729831712426233::acittaka}}, and (saññāvimokkha / asaññāvimokka) {{14729831712426233::asaññāvimokka}}
          • aṅgāni
            • veyyāvaccakaro niddisitabbo: showing an attendant to the messenger
            • saññāpetvā: messenger handing over the money to the attendant
            • uttari vāyamamāno: bhikkhu exceeding the stipulated number of prompts
            • abhinipphādeyya: receiving the robe as a result of extra attempts
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ atirekatikkhattuṃ codanāya atirekachakkhattuṃ ṭhānena abhinipphāditaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.

        • np 11 - kosiyasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Aggalāva Cetiya in the city of Āḷavī. At this time, Chabbaggiya monks approached silk-makers and stated: “Friends! Please cook more silkworms and make silk thread. May you give them to us as well. We also would like to prepare silk blankets/rugs”. Then the silkmakers criticised monks since such advice is inappropriate for monks who should abstain from causing harm to living beings. The training rule was imposed based on this incident.
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Yo pana bhikkhu kosiyamissakaṃ santhataṃ kārāpeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. (If a monk prepares a blanket/rug that contains silk thread, it will result in a nissaggiya pācittiya offence.)
          • description
            • purpose of the rule→the Tathāgata prohibited bhikkhus from preparing blankets or rugs using such thread as it would indirectly encourage silkworms to be cooked; this rule shows the Buddha's consideration for the implications of the process behind the production of products
          • pāḷi terms
            • santhata (non-woven blanket/rug/covering)
              • according to the commentaries, a santhata is like a mat / rug that can be used for sitting and lying down and carried here and there made with layers of thread stacked on top of each other (any type of thread), and by sprinkling gruel on its surface; it is not woven; santhata mentioned in other training rules are also non-woven rugs
              • kosa↔cocoon
              • kosiya↔thread prepared by cooking silkworms
              • kosiyakāraka↔one who makes the silk, silk-maker, or silk-worm
          • instances of offenses
            • preparing or making others prepare a blanket, mixing silk thread: {{06570485861705522::dkṭ}} once the making of the blanket is complete: {{06570485861705522::np}} if only a single silk thread carried by the wind ends up on it: {{06570485861705522::np}} this offence is (cittaka / acittaka?) {{06570485861705522::acittaka}} and (saññāvimokkha / nosaññāvimokkha?) {{06570485861705522::nosaññāvimokkha}} making it for another unknowingly using silk: {{06570485861705522::dkṭ for preliminary steps and dkṭ when concluded}} making use of one woven by another: {{06570485861705522::dkṭ}} making robes or other items such as canopy, a carpet, a wall screen, a mattress, or a pillow using silk thread: {{06570485861705522::no offense (maybe because it is senāsana)}} weaving blankets using silk thread: {{06570485861705522::no offense }}{{06570485861705522::(because technically it only applies to santhata which is not woven; however, when considering the reasons for promulgating the training rule, it is obvious that abstaining from weaving silk rugs is commendable)}}
          • aṅgāni
            • kosiyamissakaṁ: silk thread having been mixed
            • santhataṁ kārāpeyya: Preparing or getting it prepared for oneself
              • completing the covering
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, kosiyamissakaṃ santhataṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ ayasmato nissajjāmi.
        • np 12 - suddhakāḷakasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Kūṭāgāra hall in the city of Vesalī. At that time Chabbaggiya monks were making rugs entirely out of black goat wool (or fur); people who had been on pilgrimage happened to see this and criticised the act; bhikkhus who heard this, informed the Buddha about it, and he declared this training rule.
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Yo pana bhikkhu suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ santhataṃ kārāpeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. If a monk prepares a blanket only out of black goat wool, it will result in a nissaggiya pācittiya offence.
          • description of the training rule
            • preparing or making another prepare a santhata with only black wool: {{532237942234052::dkṭ}} once it is completed: {{532237942234052::np}} if it is done with coloured wool but completely covered by black wool: {{532237942234052::np}} doing it for another: {{532237942234052::dkṭ for the efforts and dkṭ once completed}} using one made by another: {{532237942234052::dkṭ}} if a canopy (vitāna), a carpet (bhummattharaṇa), a wallscreen (sāṇipākāra), a mattress (bhisi) or a pillow (bibbohana) is made purely out of black goat wool: {{532237942234052::no offense}}
          • pāḷi terms
            • vitānaṁ (nt.) [vi + √tan + *a] ✓↔canopy, awning; cover; lit. stretching out
            • bhūmattharaṇa / bhummattharaṇa↔carpet
            • sāṇipākāra↔wallscreen, tapestry (mem aid: "sunny wall")
            • bhisi↔mattress (mem aid: uma bici na cama)
            • bibbohana↔pillow
          • aṅgāni
            • suddhakālakānaṁ eḷakalomānaṁ: constituting of only black goat wool
            • kārāpeyya: preparing or getting it prepared for oneself
              • completing the blanket
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ santhataṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ ayasmato nissajjāmi.
          • notes:
            • elakaloma could mean fur or wool
            • in myanmar it is sheep wool, in sri lanka goat wool
        • np 13 - dvebhāgasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Jetavana temple near the city of Sāvatthi. At that time, since the Buddha had prohibited making rugs using only black goat wool, Chabbaggiya monks, in order to avoid the offence, were making rugs using a larger percentage of black goat wool and a lesser percentage of goat wool of different colours. People who had been on pilgrimage happened to see this and had been criticising the act. Bhikkhus who heard this, informed the Buddha about it, and He declared the following training rule.
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Navaṃ pana bhikkhunā santhataṃ kārayamānena dve bhāgā suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ ādātabbā tatiyaṃ odātānaṃ catutthaṃ gocariyānaṃ. Anādā ce bhikkhu dve bhāge suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ tatiyaṃ odātānaṃ catutthaṃ gocariyānaṃ navaṃ santhataṃ kārāpeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. (If a monk prepares a new blanket, he must obtain two parts of black goat wool, one part of white goat wool and another one part of brown goat wool. If a new blanket is made outside this formula using black goat wool more than stipulated, it will result in a nissaggiya pācittiya offence.)
          • description
            • If a santhata is being made the amount of black wool that is taken must be {{2656766654579614::2 quarters or less (dvebhāgā)}} of the total wool requirement by weight; the rest must be of other colors such as white or brown (it does not matter the percentage of which extra color) making it with more black wool than that: {{2656766654579614::dkṭ during the process and np when completed}} making it or having it made for another using more black wool than the stipulated: {{2656766654579614::dkṭ during the process and dkṭ when completed}} using one made by another: {{2656766654579614::dkṭ}} making a vitāna (canopy), bhummattharaṇa (carpet), sāṇipākāra (wallscreen), bhisi (mattress) or a pillow (bibbohana) using more black wool than the stipulated: {{2656766654579614::no offense}} making it while not being aware of there being more black wool than the stipulated: {{2656766654579614::np}} this offense is (sacittaka / acittaka?) {{2656766654579614::acittaka}} and (saññāvimokkha / nosaññāvimokkha?) {{2656766654579614::nosaññāvimokkha}}
          • aṅgāni
            • dvebhāgā suddhakāḷakānaṁ eḷakalomānaṁ...: having included black wool more than the specified quantity (more than half)
            • kārayamānena: reparing or getting it prepared for oneself
              • completing the rug
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, santhataṃ anādiyitvā dve tule suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ tulaṃ odātānaṃ tulaṃ gocariyānaṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ ayasmato nissajjāmi.
          • note:
            • what happens to the nissaggiya items under np11 (kosiya), 12 (suddhakālaka) and 13 (eḷakaloma) after the nissajjana is done?→the item cannot be used by the monk who made the santhata
        • np 14 - chabbassasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Jetavana monastery near the city of Sāvatthi. At that time, most bhikkhus in Sāvatthi were in the habit of getting new blankets done every year. Monks often asked for goat wool and demanded for it saying “Give us goat wool” (dehi me elakalomaṁ...) or “We are in need of goat wool.” (elakalomena me attho) (both of these are viññatti); (in rāja there is a difference, no difference in their power, in that sikkha the buddha said which is appropriate; more suitable but both are viññatti; ) This resulted in criticism of the bhikkhus by laymen. The Tathāgata who learnt about this matter declared a training rule prohibiting monks from making a new blanket before elapsing six years from when one blanket is done. At that time, one monk became ill in the city of Kosambhi. His relatives sent a messenger to accompany him to be brought to be cared for. This particular bhikkhu did not go because new blankets could not be made, his old blanket could not be taken and it was difficult for him to be without a blanket. The Tathāgata who got to know about this declared: “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa bhikkhuno santhatasammutiṃ dātuṃ”, “I allow the Saṅgha to give an allowance to a sick monk to make a new rug within six years” and amended the rule
            • notes:
              • what are the rules related to gilānasammuti?→uddosita (np2), chabbassa (np14), sāsaṅkha (np29)
              • in sekhiya, gilāna is anāpatti, not sammuti
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Navaṃ pana bhikkhunā santhataṃ kārāpetvā chabbassāni dhāretabbaṃ. Orena ce channaṃ vassānaṃ taṃ santhataṃ vissajjetvā vā avissajjetvā vā aññaṃ navaṃ santhataṃ kārāpeyya, aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. A monk must consume a new blanket which he made or got someone else to make for six years. Therefore, if a monk gets a new blanket made, having or not having given up the original rug before the lapse of six years, without a bhikkhu sammuti, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will be committed.
          • description of the training rule
            • a santhata should be used for a period of {{015242360415399281::six years}} making a new one before the pasing of six years from the day the last one was made: {{015242360415399281::dkṭ for the process and np when concluded}} making it on or after the day 6 years are completed: {{015242360415399281::no offense}} the counting is done by the moon calendar if sick a monk may obtain a {{015242360415399281::gilānasammuti}} and may make new santhatas every {{015242360415399281::year}} when recovered, the sammuti does not apply, but once again sick it automatically applies once again reagardless of the kind of sickness making it for someone else before the six years: {{015242360415399281::no offense}} receiving, using a second santhata made by another before the 6 year period is over: {{015242360415399281::no offense}} if a canopy, a carpet, a wall screen, a mattress, or a pillow is made within the six years: {{015242360415399281::no offence}} making one mistakenly believing 6 years have passed: {{015242360415399281::np}} this training rule is (acittaka / sacittaka?) {{015242360415399281::acittaka}} and (saññāvimokkha / nosaññāvimokkha?) {{015242360415399281::nosaññāvimokka}}
            • comparing santhatas
              • kosiya santhata (np1) making for another: {{5685330955438559::dkṭ}} using one made by others: {{5685330955438559::dkṭ}} suddhakālaka santhata (np2) making for another: {{5685330955438559::dkṭ}} using one made by others: {{5685330955438559::dkṭ}} atirekadvebhāga santhata (np3) making for another: {{5685330955438559::dkṭ}} using one made by others: {{5685330955438559::dkṭ}} ūnakachabbassa santhata (np4) making for another: {{5685330955438559::anāpatti}} using one made by others: {{5685330955438559::anāpatti}} nisīdana santhata (np5) making for another: {{5685330955438559::dkṭ}} using one made by others: {{5685330955438559::anāpatti}}
          • aṅgāni
            • orena ce channaṃ vassānaṃ: making or getting the blanket made before the designated time period
            • aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā: not having obtained the gilānasammuti
            • kārāpetvā: preparing or getting it prepared for oneself
              • completing the blanket
          • nissajjana
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, santhataṃ ūnakachabbassāni kārāpitaṃ, aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā, nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ ayasmato nissajjāmi
        • np 15 - nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpada
          • background
            • the agreement the Tathāgata was residing at the {{5876846637346893::Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika's park, Sāvatthi}} when He informed the monks He would go into seclusion and only the one who would bring piṇḍapāta could approach Him; monks made an agreement that one who approach Him would be committing a {{5876846637346893::pācittiya offense}}; the visit then {{5876846637346893::Vaṅgantaputta Upasena Thera}} approached the Buddha together with his students and after having a cordial conversation they discussed the fact that {{5876846637346893::one of the monks in the assembly was wearing a paṁsukūla robe he did not like because of following his teacher's practice}}; the Buddha praised the monks and inquired about Upasena's training to which he said he only ordained or gave nissaya to those who could follow his practices of {{5876846637346893::araññikaṅga, piṇḍapātikaṅga and paṁsukūlikaṅga}}; the Buddha praised him; the allowance He then inquired about the monk's agreement; the ven. explained it and said {{5876846637346893::he only abided by the rules promulgated by the Buddha}} which the Buddha praised, giving the monks who followed those austerities the allowance to approach Him as they wish; informing the others the ven. then informed the others of their fault and of the allowance, leading many to observe austerities; some while undertaking tecīvarikaṅga discarded their santhatas believing it to be a hindrance for it; promulgation of the rule emerging from seclusion and wandering through the monastery, the Buddha noticed many discarded santhatas and promulgated the rule mem aid: for Vaṅgantaputta Upasena, and araññika, piṇḍapātika and paṁsukūlikaṅga
            • do santhatas have to be determined?→a non-woven rug is not necessary to be determined, so technically, keeping one does not break the tecīvarikaṅga dhutaṅga
          • training rule in pāḷi
            • Nisīdanasanthataṃ pana bhikkhunā kārayamānena purāṇasanthatassa sāmantā sugatavidatthi ādātabbā dubbaṇṇakaraṇāya, anādā ce bhikkhu purāṇasanthatassa sāmantā sugatavidatthiṃ navaṃ nisīdanasanthataṃ kārāpeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. A monk getting a sitting-rug made, should take a piece of cloth of the size of a sugata handspan, from an old rug for the purpose of discolouring the sitting-rug. If a monk gets a new sitting-rug made without obtaining a piece of cloth of the size of a sugata hand span, from an old rug, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will be committed.
          • description of the training rule
            • When a bhikkhu makes or orders a new nisīdanasanthata to be made, and if he has an old santhata, he must incorporate a piece of cloth of the size of {{14137350091670164::a sugata handspan}} from the latter. This is done so to make use of the old santhata when a new nisīdana santhata is made after six years from the manufacturing date of the old existing santhata. If a bhikkhu makes a new sitting-rug while the old rug can still be made use of and without taking a piece of cloth of such size from it, a {{14137350091670164::np}} offence will be committed if the old one is completely destroyed: {{14137350091670164::one does not have to use it}}
            • note:
              • whether can nisidanasanthata be made before 6 years is not clear
              • the purpose is to use the material of the old one that is still usable, if all destroyed no need to use
          • Nisīdana santhata (non-woven sitting-rug)
            • a nisīdana santhata is a santhata that has borders like in a normal nisīdana. Therefore, the definition of nisīdana santhata is given in the padabhājanīya as, “Nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ (with borders) vuccati. Santhataṃ nāma santharitvā kataṃ hoti avāyimaṃ. ”Therefore, nisīdana santhata is a rug that is not woven, but with borders. This too needs not to be determined like a non-woven santhata. It is mentioned in sub-commentaries that some scholars held the idea that nisīdana santhata and nisīdana cīvara are identical. But Vimativinodanī does not appreciate this idea.
            • note:
              • some teachers think (not strongly refuted but not appreciated) but comm thinks not the same as nisīdana for sitting;
              • size not mentioned
              • normal santhata is not woven
          • The procedure of making a nisīdana santhata and how and how not offences are committed
            • The portion of cloth that must be taken from the old rug to the new sitting-rug can be either in the form of a circle or a square. If the portion is a circle, its {{6161144944113413::diameter}} must be at least {{6161144944113413::one Sugata handspan}}, if a square, {{6161144944113413::the length of one side must be at least a Sugata handspan}}. It can be attached to one or several sides of the new sitting-rug. For some reason if the designated size cannot be extracted from the old rug, it is allowed to {{6161144944113413::take a piece that is smaller than a Sugata handspan}}. If the old rug is totally destroyed, an offence will not be committed if the new sitting-rug is made or ordered to be made without obtaining a single piece from the old santhata. As indicated in the Vinaya Pāḷi, if a new sitting-rug is made or ordered to be made for another without taking a piece of cloth of the size of a Sugata hand span from the old rug, the bhikkhu will be committing {{6161144944113413::dukkaṭa offences while making efforts and at the completion of the rug}}. Consuming such a sitting-rug prepared by another {{6161144944113413::will not result in an offence}}.11 A canopy, a carpet, a wall screen, a mattress, or a pillow is made or ordered to be made without taking a piece of cloth the size of a Sugata handspan from the old santhata, {{6161144944113413::it will not result in any offence}}. This is an (acittaka / sacittaka?) {{6161144944113413::acittaka}}, (saññāvimokkha / nosaññāvimokkha?) {{6161144944113413::nosaññāvimokkha}} offence
          • Factors
            • purāṇasanthatassa sāmantā sugatavidatthi ādātabbā: not taking a piece of cloth the size of a Sugata handspan from the old santhata when it is possible to do so
            • kārayamānena: preparing or getting it prepared for oneself
            • nisīdanasanthataṁ: completing the sitting-rug
          • Forfeiture
            • Idaṃ me, bhante, nisīdanasanthataṃ anādiyitvā purāṇasanthatassa sāmantā sugatavidatthiṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.
          • note: not sure if it has to be used for a new santhata, the rules is about nisīdanasanthata
        • np 16 - eḷakalomasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Jetavana temple near the city of Sāvatthi. At this time, a bhikkhu who was on his way to Sāvatthi received goat fur (or wool). He made a pile of it, covered it with his upper robe and carried it. The people who saw this asked him mockingly: “How much have you taken? What is the profit you made?” This made the bhikkhu feel shy and speechless. The Buddha who came to know about this incident declared this training rule.
          • Training rule in Pali
            • Bhikkhuno paneva addhānamaggappaṭipannassa eḷakalomāni uppajjeyyuṃ. Ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabbāni. Paṭiggahetvā tiyojanaparamaṃ sahatthā haritabbāni, asante hārake. Tato ce uttari hareyya, asantepi hārake, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. If a monk receives goat fur while travelling, he may accept it if desired. Once accepted, if there’s no one else to carry it, he can only carry it by himself, up to three yojanas. If he happens to carry it beyond the limit of three yojanas in the absence of a carrier, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will occur.
          • Description of the training rule
            • A bhikkhu who receives goat fur must not carry it beyond {{9826691569749155::three yojanas}} by himself. The Tathāgata imposed this training rule because it is inappropriate for bhikkhus to do so. When taken the goat fur beyond three yojanas, the goat fur becomes {{9826691569749155::nissaggiya}} while the bhikkhu will have committed a {{9826691569749155::pācittiya}} offence. When the three-yojana boundary is passed, by taking the initial step therein, a {{9826691569749155::dukkaṭa}} offence will be committed. {{9826691569749155::Pācittiya}} offence will be committed upon the second step. The bhikkhu can carry the goat fur within the {{9826691569749155::three-yojana}} distance without committing any offence.
            • If the goat fur is carried back and forth within the area between the location of receiving the goat fur and the three-yojana mark, even if the monk walks more than three yojanas in total, {{5069783648336348::there is no offense}}. An offence will not be committed under this training rule as long as the monk does not cross the threeyojana boundary (from the receiving location). If the bhikkhu who received the goat fur gets another person to carry it, passing the three-yojana boundary will {{5069783648336348::not result in an offence}}. Further, it should be known that carrying an object made out of goat fur will {{5069783648336348::not result in an offence}}
            • if the initial three-yojana mark is crossed while carrying fur that is stolen by thieves and returned, and while carrying goat fur that has been returned after being forfeited through the nissajjana vinayakamma {{18109269204126632::an offence will not occur}}. If the goat fur is received this way and had to be carried again, an additional three yojanas can be covered from the point of the second receiving. The initial three-yojana mark is not taken into consideration. This is the opinion demonstrated in the Gaṇṭhipada and Vimativinodanī. According to the Sāratthadīpanī, there is no limit in the distance the goat fur could be carried when received the second time.
            • If the goat fur is received in one particular place, a distance of three yojanas can be travelled forward from thereon, and take up residence therein. From that point onwards, goat fur can be carried for another three yojanas. This training rule is {{4658933700398924::acittaka}} and {{4658933700398924::nosaññāvimokkha}}. Even if one is unaware of or doubting the distance travelled while the three yojana miles are exceeded, an offence {{4658933700398924::will occur}}
          • Factors
            • 1. Goat fur that has not been made into an object
            • 2. Receiving it for the first time
            • 3. Passing the three-yojana mark
            • 4. Not being a journey in which the monk travels more than three yojana back and forth within the three-yojana boundary.
            • 5. Not a journey that was initiated after residing in a place within the three-yojana boundary after the first receiving
          • Forfeiture
            • Imāni me, bhante, eḷakalomāni tiyojanaṃ atikkāmitāni nissaggiyāni. Imānāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.
        • np 17 - eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpada
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Nigrodha monastery in the city of Kapilavatthu. At this time, Chabbaggiya monks got bhikkhunis to wash goat fur. They even asked them to dye and untangle them (card the wool). This resulted in the deterioration of the bhikkhunis' Dhamma studies and training of adhisīla, adhicitta and adhipaññā. Mahā Pajāpatī Gotamī informed this matter to the Buddha one day. As a result, this training rule was declared.
          • Training rule in Pali
            • Yo pana bhikkhu aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā eḷakalomāni dhovāpeyya vā rajāpeyya vā vijaṭāpeyya vā, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. If a monk gets an unrelated bhikkhuni to wash or dye or untangle (card) goat fur, a nissaggiya pācittiya offence will be committed
          • Description of the training rule
            • If a bhikkhu asks an unrelated bhikkhuni to wash or dye or untangle goat fur owned by him, it will result in a {{7070308360194955::pācittiya}} offence for the bhikkhu while the goat fur will become {{7070308360194955::nissaggiya}}. The rest of the information pertaining to this training rule must be understood as per the {{7070308360194955::purāṇacīvara training rule (np4)}}
          • Factors
            • eḷakalomāni: being fur / wool
            • aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā: ordering an unrelated bhikkhuni who is in the vicinity of twelve cubits (upacāra)
            • dhovāpeyya vā rajāpeyya vā vijaṭāpeyya vā: the same bhikkhuni executing any of the three tasks, i.e., washing, dyeing and carding (combing out, untangling)
          • Forfeiture
            • Imāni me, bhante, eḷakalomāni aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā dhovāpitāni (rajāpitāni/vijaṭāpitāni) nissaggiyāni. Imānāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmi.
        • np 18 - rūpiyasikkhāpadaṃ
          • background
            • The Tathāgata was residing at the Veḷuvana monastery in the city of Rājagaha. At this time, Venerable Upananda, a son of Sākyans became friendly with a certain family. If any food or drink item is prepared in that house, Upananda Thera also had a portion set aside for him. One day, meat was prepared in the evening in this household. Even though Venerable Upananda’s portion was reserved, it had to be given to the child in the house who was crying early in the morning. When Venerable Upananda arrived at the household, the matter was explained and had been asked what kind of meat he would like for the value of one gold coin. Then Venerable Upananda, instead of mentioning the preferred meat, requested the gold coin. The householder was displeased and started bad-mouthing the bhikkhu. When this matter was informed, the Buddha imposed the rūpiya training rule.
            • note:
              • money is the cause / root of all requisites
          • Training rule in Pali
            • Yo pana bhikkhu jātarūparajataṃ uggaṇheyya vā uggaṇhāpeyya vā upanikkhittaṃ vā sādiyeyya nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. If a monk accepts gold, silver or money (rūpiya) himself or gets someone else to accept on his behalf or maintains silence implying acceptance when kept in front of him to offer him, the rūpiya must be forfeited. A pācittiya offence will be committed.
          • Description of the training rule
            • Jātarūpa specifically denotes {{5828879301133194::gold}}, while in certain contexts, the term "rajata" pertains to {{5828879301133194::silver}}. In this instance, "rajata" refers to {{5828879301133194::not only silver but also encompasses various forms of currency employed in trade apart from gold}}. A comprehensive term for these precious mediums is "rūpiya," encompassing {{5828879301133194::gold, silver, and currency fashioned from diverse metals, paper or any other material, all intended for use in transactions}}. The training rule is breached when a monk accepts or makes someone accept on his behalf rūpiya that is directly offered to him or collects or makes someone collect on his behalf rūpiya that has been discarded. When rūpiya is kept close to the bhikkhu with the intention of offering, and if the bhikkhu does not reject the offering by a gesture or words or at least with a rejecting thought: “These are not allowable to us,” and remains to be tacitly approving, a {{5828879301133194::nissaggiya pācittiya}} offence will be committed.
          • Akappiya vatthu, kappiya vatthu and related offences
            • all physical things, according to Vinaya, are categorised into two groups (vatthu) according to their inherent nature of being allowable or not for monks
              • kappiyavatthu / arūpiya - objects that are allowable for monks to accept ((piṇḍapāta, robes, umbrella, slippers...)
              • akappiyavatthu - objects which if accepted a monk entails an offense
                • dukkaṭavatthu - objects which if accepted a monk entails a dukkaṭa offence (8 / 15)
                • nissaggiyavatthu / rūpiya - objects which if accepted a monk entails a nissaggiyapācittiya offence (3): rūpiya, jātarūpa, rajata (gold, silver and currencies)
              • note:
                • jātarūpa→gold
                • rajata↔silver in most contexts but here any currency made of any material as well
                • rūpiya↔jātarūparajata
            • 8 / 15 dukkaṭavatthu
              • 1 - 8 'precious items' (muttādi)
                • 1. Mutta - Pearl
                • 2. Maṇi - Gems
                • 3. Viḷuriya - Lapis lazuli
                • 4. Saṅkha - Chank and conch shells
                • 5. Silā - Quartz
                • 6. Pavāla - Corals
                • 7. Lohitaṅka - Ruby
                • 8. Māsāragalla - cat’s eye
              • 9. Satta dhañña - Seven types of grains (with the husk)

              • 11. Khetta - Paddy fields
              • 12. Pupphārāma - Flower gardens
              • 13. Phalārāma - Orchards

                  • taḷākaṁ nt.↔lake; pond; pool; dam
                  • vāpī fem.↔reservoir; dam; pond
