    • ariyadhana
      • gāthā:
        • "saddhādhanaṁ sīladhanaṁ hiriottappiyaṁ dhanaṁ, sutadhanañca cāgo ca paññā me sattamaṁ dhanaṁ, yassa ete dhanā atthi itthiyā purisassa vā, adaḷiddoti taṁ āhu amoghaṁ tassa jīvitaṁ" (they say that one who has these seven wealths, be it a man or woman, he/she is not poor and his/her life is not empty)
      • saddhādhanaṁ: believing in the Buddha and kamma-vipāka sīladhanaṁ: protecting at least the 5 precepts hiridhanaṁ: despising immorality ottappadhanaṁ: fear of immorality sutadhanaṁ: knowledge of dhamma cāgadhanaṁ: donating paññādhanaṁ: intelligence
      • 2 types of wealth, which is higher and why
        • material wealth
        • wealth of virtues
        • note: wealth of virtues is higher because material wealth is easily lost, causes harm to the owner, divides people, etc, and the wealth of virtues helps acquire all other material things and supramundane dhamma
    • aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo
      • "pabbajitvāna kātena pāpakammaṁ vivajjayi, vacīduccaritaṁ hitvā ājīvaṁ parisodhayi" (suttanipāta 410) (having renounced, he abandoned bodily evil, and after abandoning verbal misconduct he purified his livelihood) (said of Siddhattha)
      • 1. Sammādiṭṭhi – right view (insight of four noble truth)
        • I. Dukkhe ñāṇaṃ = knowledge of suffering,
        • II. Dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ = knowledge of cause of suffering,
        • III. Dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ = knowledge of the cessation of suffering,
        • IV. dukkhanirodhagāminiyāpaṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ = knowledge of path that leads to get free from suffering
      • 2. Sammā saṅkappo: right thoughts, right intention
        • I. Nekkhammasaṅkappo = intention of renunciation, the thought of letting go of sensual pleasure.
        • II. Abyāpādasaṅkappo = intention of good will, thought of non-hatred
        • III. Avihiṃsāsaṅkappo = intention of harmlessness.
      • 3. Sammāvācā: right speech
        • I. Musāvādāveramaṇī = refraining from lying
        • II. Pisuṇāvācā – veramaṇī = refraining from slanderous speech
        • III. Pharusāvācā – veramaṇī = refraining from harsh speech
        • IV. Sampapphalāpā – veramaṇī = frivolous speech, idle speech
      • 4. Sammākammanta: right action
        • I. Pāṇātipātāveramaṇī = refraining from killing beings.
        • II. Adinnādānāveramaṇī = refraining from stealing
        • III. Kāmesumicchācārā-veramaṇī/Abrahmacariyāveramaṇī = refraining from sexual misconducts/ sexual activities.
      • 5. Sammā ājīva: right livelihood (micchā ājīvaṃ pahāya sammāājīvena jīvitaṁ kappeti)
        • I. Right living by avoiding from wrong earning (vaṇijjā)
        • II. Right gaining of four requisites.
      • 6. Sammā vāyāma: right effort
        • I. Effort to prevent arising of un-arisen defilements.
        • II. Effort to abandon of arisen defilements.
        • III. Effort to arouse un-arisen wholesome states.
        • IV. Effort to develop arisen wholesome states.
      • 7. Sammā sati: right mindfulness on four satipaṭṭhāna;
        • I. Kāyānupassanā – mindfulness on the body as that really are
        • II. Vedanānupassanā – mindfulness on the feeling as they really are.
        • III. Cittānupassanā – mindfulness on mind as they really are.
        • IV. Dhammānupassanā – mindfulness on dhamma (phenomenon) as they really are.
      • 8. Sammā samādhi: right concentration
        • I. Fist jhāna
        • II. Second jhāna
        • III. Third jhāna
        • IV. Forth jhāna
        • note: Concentration freed from hindrances (vinīvaraṇa-citta) can include
          • • Upacāra-samādhi
          • • Khaṇika samādhi – kalla-citta, mudu-citta, (soft and active)
      • Two extremes: not encouraged to follow
        • 1. Kāmasukallikānuyogo = indulging sensual pleasure as a form of liberation
        • 2. Attakilamathānuyogo = self-mortification
    • catusacca
      • 1. Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ: noble truth of suffering:
        • Meaning of word “dukkha” {{17518995724467734::“du” represent a prefix refers to something that is dispicable, disgusting (kucchita), “kha” empty, void (tuccha). Something void of essence.}}
        • 3 types of dukkha
          • a. Dukkha-dukkha: reality that represent physical and mental pain known as suffering.
          • b. Vipariṇāma-dukkha: reality that bring suffering due to change.
          • c. Saṅkhāra-dukkha: the reality that bring suffering due to conditionality
        • 4 senses / aspects of dukkha:
          • i. Pīḷanaṭṭho – in the sense of oppressed
          • ii. Saṅkhataṭṭho – in the sense of conditioned
          • iii. Santāpaṭṭho – in the sense of exhausted
          • iv. Viparināmaṭṭho – in the sense of arisen and fallen
      • 2. Dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccam: noble truth of cause of suffering.
        • Saṃ= saṃyoga (coming together), U = uppatti (becoming) and Aya = kāraṇa (condition).
        • So taṅhā is the main cause of arising of suffering (cause of bhāva). It is three types:
          • a. Kāmataṅhā – craving for sensual pleasure.
          • b. Bhavataṅhā – craving for existence.
          • c. Vibhavataṅhā - craving for annihilation.
        • Four senses / aspects of the cause of suffering:
          • i. āyūhanaṭṭho - in the sense of grasping
          • ii. nidānaṭṭho - in the sense of cause
          • iii. saṃyogaṭṭho – in the sense of attachment
          • iv. paḷibodhaṭṭho - in the sense of impediment
          • mem aid:
          • vocab:
            • aṭṭha [√ar + tha] (m.)↔goal; purpose; meaning; sense
      • 3. Dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ: noble truth of cessation of suffering.
        • Ni= negate something, rodha = cārakaṃ (prison). Freed of prison which is round of rebirth is nirodha. That is the cessation of the craving or Nibbāna.
        • Four aspects of cessation:
          • i. Nissaraṇaṭṭho – escape
          • ii. Vivekaṭṭho – peace
          • iii. Asaṅkataṭṭho – unconditioned
          • iv. Amataṭṭho - deathless
      • 4. Dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ.
        • {{5468148127507979::Maggati gacchatīti }}Maggo (it is call magga in the meaning of walking toward. In other word paṭipadā (training, practice).
        • Yasmā panetaṃ ariyasaccaṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati ārammaṇavasena tadabhimukhabhūtattā, paṭipadā ca hoti dukkhanirodhappattiyā, tasmā "dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā"ti vuccati. By this (paṭipadā) goes toward nibbana by taking nibbana as object, therefore it is called path. Basically eight path factors are taken.
        • Four aspects of the path:
          • i. Nīyānaṭṭho – vehicle
          • ii. Hetuṭṭho – by means of reason
          • iii. Dassanaṭṭho – by means of vision
          • iv. Adhipateyyaṭṭho – by means of authority

              • 4 types of "love" #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • attapema (self-love): connected to the natural instinct of survival; when strong it may lead to selfishness, and in extreme cases, this selfcenteredness can lead someone to harm or even kill others in order to protect themselves. “{{914552542939246::natthi attasamaṃ pemaṃ}}” (There is no love equal to self-love)
                • lustful love (rāga): connected to the natural reproductive instincts; when one gets what one wants it is considered successful but when not it leads to resentment; Pemasutta: cattārimāni, bhikkhave, (pemāni) jāyanti. katamāni cattāri? {{6283674367332961::pemā pemaṃ jāyati, pemā doso jāyati, dosā pemaṃ jāyati, dosā doso jāyati}} ((1) love is born of love, (2) hate is born of love, (3) love is born of hate, and and (4) hate is born of hate)
                  • pemasuttaṃ:
                    • "cattārimāni, bhikkhave, (pemāni) jāyanti. katamāni cattāri? pemā pemaṃ jāyati, pemā doso jāyati, dosā pemaṃ jāyati, dosā doso jāyati. "kathañca, bhikkhave, pemā pemaṃ jāyati? idha, bhikkhave, puggalo puggalassa iṭṭho hoti kanto manāpo. taṃ pare iṭṭhena kantena manāpena samudācaranti. tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘yo kho myāyaṃ puggalo iṭṭho kanto manāpo, taṃ pare iṭṭhena kantena manāpena samudācarantī’ti. so tesu pemaṃ janeti. evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pemā pemaṃ jāyati. "kathañca, bhikkhave, pemā doso jāyati? idha, bhikkhave, puggalo puggalassa iṭṭho hoti kanto manāpo. taṃ pare aniṭṭhena akantena amanāpena samudācaranti. tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘yo kho myāyaṃ puggalo iṭṭho kanto manāpo, taṃ pare aniṭṭhena akantena amanāpena samudācarantī’ti. so tesu dosaṃ janeti. evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pemā doso jāyati. "kathañca, bhikkhave, dosā pemaṃ jāyati? idha, bhikkhave, puggalo puggalassa aniṭṭho hoti akanto amanāpo. taṃ pare aniṭṭhena akantena amanāpena samudācaranti. tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘yo kho myāyaṃ puggalo aniṭṭho akanto amanāpo, taṃ pare aniṭṭhena akantena amanāpena samudācarantī’ti. so tesu pemaṃ janeti. evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dosā pemaṃ jāyati. "kathañca, bhikkhave, dosā doso jāyati? idha, bhikkhave, puggalo puggalassa aniṭṭho hoti akanto amanāpo. taṃ pare iṭṭhena kantena manāpena samudācaranti. tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘yo kho myāyaṃ puggalo aniṭṭho akanto amanāpo, taṃ pare iṭṭhena kantena manāpena samudācarantī’ti. so tesu dosaṃ janeti. evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dosā doso jāyati. imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri pemāni jāyanti.

            • background #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • once, the Blessed One was staying in {{4955221040580262::Sāvatthī}} ; before the rains retreat He explained various meditation subjects that would suit the {{4955221040580262::84,000}} different types of temperaments (mainly rāga, dosa, moha, vitakka, saddhā and buddhi caritas); a group of 500 monks, after learning their meditation subjects, took His permission and went in search of a suitable place to dwell; wandering by stages they reached {{4955221040580262::a mountain in the Himalayas made of nīla stones, shady forests, silver-like sand, and pools of pure water}}; the nearby village of a {{4955221040580262::1.000}} faithful families welcomed them and invited them to spend the retreat there, building them huts with all needs; after accepting the invitation they remained there practicing diligently; their radiance surpassed that of the tree deities and the deities had to descend from their mansions and roam about; displeased the monks would stay for 3 months, they {{4955221040580262::conjured up frightening sights and sounds, and unpleasant odors, disturbing their practice and causing them bodily and mental distress}}; one day in conclave the elder brought up the issue and they decided to return to the Blessed One for guidance; after proper investigation the Blessed One gave them instructions on how a forest-dwelling monk should practice; there should be two sessions, one in the morning and one in the evening, of the following: {{4955221040580262::mettā, protective discourses, foulness, recollection of death and attention to the eight important reminders}}; after that He taught the mettasutta for cultivating loving-kindness, for their protection and for serving as a vipassanāpadakajjhāna, and sent them back to the very same place. mem aid: In Sāvatthi, before the rains, the Buddha explains kammaṭṭhānas, a group of 500 goes to a mountain and while dwelling there is disturbed by local devas; taking advice from the Buddha they listen to the mettasutta and return to that place
            • 3 purposes of the mettāsutta
              • mettattha - for the purpose of loving-kindness
              • parittattha - for the purpose of protection
              • vipassanāpadakajjhānattha - for the purpose of using the jhāna as a base for vipassanā
            • a forest dweller (āraññakena) should know
              • "apica kho āraññakena pariharaṇaṃ ñātabbaṃ. seyyathidaṃ – sāyaṃ pātaṃ karaṇavasena dve mettā dve parittā dve asubhā dve maraṇassatī aṭṭhamahāsaṃvegavatthusamāvajjanañca, aṭṭha mahāsaṃvegavatthūni nāma jātijarābyādhimaraṇaṃ cattāri apāyadukkhānīti, atha vā jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhaṁ" "A monk who resides in the forest should know how to proceed. In the evening and morning, there should be two sessions of practicing loving-kindness (mettā), two recitations of protection (Paritta), two sessions of contemplating the unattractive nature of the body (asubha), two sessions of mindfulness of death (maraṇānussati), and attention to the eight important reminders (aṭṭhamahāsaṃvegavatthu). The eight important reminders are: birth, old age, illness, death, and the suffering in the four unhappy realms. Alternatively, the first four are birth, old age, illness, and death, followed by the suffering in the unhappy realm, the suffering resulting from past actions, the suffering anticipated in future lives, and the suffering arising from the struggle to find food in the present."

          • themes addressed in the mettasutta #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • short version:
              • 1st verse to the first half of the 3rd verse: virtues
              • 2nd half of the 3rd verse to the 9th verse: mettābhāvanā
              • 10th verse: vipassanā
            • detailed version:
              • 1st half of the 1st verse: what should be done and should not be done
              • 2nd half of the 1st verse, 2nd and 3rd verses: 15 great qualities and 1st method of mettā (sabbasaṅgahakamettā)
              • 4th and 5th verses: development based on pairs (dukamettā) and triads (tikamettā)
              • 6th verse: 3 pakiṇṇakamettā
              • 7th verse: how genuine mettā should be developed
              • 8th verse: no boundaries, no enemies
              • 9th verse: no fixed posture
              • 10th verse: how to attain the noble path & fruition with mettābhāvanā

"{{6722389546261811::This should be done by the one skillful in beneficial practices, who wishes to attain penetrative realization of peaceful state; he is to be able, upright, very upright, compliant, pliant, not conceited}}" #[[khuddaka exam]]

          • karaṇīyaṁ (what should be done) #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • 3 sikkhā #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • adhisīla-sikkhā (training in higher morality): upasampadā sīla
              • adhicitta-sikkhā (training in higher mentality): aṭṭhasamāpatti as a base for vipassanā
              • adhipaññā-sikkhā (training in higher wisdom): vipassanā
              • note: another explanation (not for exam): the 3 viratis in maggacitta is adhisīla; the ekaggata, sati and vīriya are adhicitta; the amoha and vitakka are adhipaññā
            • akaraṇīyaṁ (what should not be done): the four vipattis (defects / failures): #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • sīlavipatti (failure in morality [refers to pārājika and saṅghādisesa offenses])
              • ācāravipatti (failure in good behaviour [refers to the remaining five offenses])
              • diṭṭhivipatti (failure in views or wrong views [ten erroneous extremist views [antagāhikadiṭṭhi, etc.])
              • ājīvavipatti (failure in livelihood)

          • atthakusalena ({{6531592380731135::one skillful in what is good}}) #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • anatthakusala (one skillful in what is not good) #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • anesana: one earns one's living by any of the 21 improper means (by gifts of bamboos, leaves, flowers, fruits, toothwood, mouthwash, bathing implements, bath powder, clay; by flattery, beansoupery, and fondling; by conveying messages; by the work of a physician, by the work of a messenger, by going on errands; by presenting a portion of his almsfood as a gift; by geomancy, astrology, or palmistry)
              • agocara: one moves about in the six kinds of wrong resort (prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs and bars)
              • saṁsaṭṭha: he forms bonds with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and their disciples, in the inappropriate way that laypeople form bonds
              • assaddhādikula: he associates with, resorts to, and visits families that are without faith and confidence, that are miserly, abusive, and contemptuous, that wish for loss, harm, discomfort, and trouble
              • mem aid:
            • attha (true benefit / welfare): 4 types of sīla #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • pātimokkhasaṃvarasīla: fulfilled by saddhā
              • indriyasaṃvarasīla: not giving rise to covetousness or dejection when objects strike against the six sense doors; fulfilled by sati
              • ājīvapārisuddhisīla: obtaining requisites by righteous means; fulfilled by vīriya
              • paccayasannissitasīla: reflecting on the proper use of requisites and the four sampajañña; fulfilled by paññā
            • 3 meanings of atthakusala (one skilled in what is good) #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • one skilled in sīla: one who purifies the sīla and when reflecting on it, does not find even the slightest fault
              • one skilled in samādhi: one who exerts himself to suppress the defilements and obtains the meditative attainments
              • one skilled in paññā: one who analizes conditioned realities and attains arahantship is the foremost of those skillful in the good
              • in brief: it means one is skillful in good behavior (sīla), attainments (samādhi) and path and fruition (paññā)
          • yantasantaṁ padaṁ abhisamecca ({{638572110389996::having understood (with wordly wisdom) the peaceful state}}) #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • sakko ({{6007982506202474::able}}) #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • pañca padhāniyaṅga (factors of striving) #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • saddho hoti
              • appābādho appātaṅko
              • asaṭho hoti amāyāvī
              • āraddhavīriyo
              • paññavā (he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering)
              • note: #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • 'sakko' refers to the {{7438147721076662::2nd}}{{7438147721076662:: and }}{{7438147721076662::4th}} padhāniyaṅga 'uju' and 'suhuju' refers to the {{7438147721076662::3rd}} padhāniyaṅga
            • the king of Tāvatimsa, Sakka, got that high position by his great diligence and ability; "He is able; therefore, he is called ‘Sakka'"
          • uju (upright)
          • suhuju (very upright)
            • the difference between uju and suhuju is (4 methods) #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • uju: occasional straightforwardness or while one is young suhuju: habitual straightforwardness
              • uju: asaṭha (not showing qualities one does not possess) suhuju: amāyāvī (not hiding one's faults)
              • uju: abandoning bodily and verbal crookedness suhuju: abandoning mental crookedness
              • uju: not showing the virtues that one does not have (asaṭha) suhuju: not consenting to gains accrued due to non-existent virtues
          • suvaco (easy to admonish)
          • mudu (gentle)
            • gentle in the practice of the duties and in the entire spiritual life
            • gentle in bodily and verbal actions; one shows a joyful face, uses friendly speech with pleasant words, just like a good harbour where many ships can easily dock
            • it is mentioned that if he is asked to convey messages and go on errands, and so forth, he should not be gentle about this but should remain firm
          • anatimānī (not conceited)
            • pride of bad things is called {{3278112639974329::micchāmāna}}
              • H O M E 🏡
          • Assignment - fifteen great qualities in mettāsutta #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • by Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
            • sakko
              • One is able (sakko) when one fulfills the second and fourth factors of striving, namely appābādho appātaṅko and āraddhavīriyo
            • uju & suhuju
              • One is considered upright (uju) or very upright (suhuju) according to four methods:
                • uju: occasional uprightness or while one is young suhuju: habitual uprightness
                • uju: asaṭha (not showing qualities one does not possess) suhuju: amāyāvī (not hiding one's faults)
                • uju: abandoning bodily and verbal crookedness suhuju: abandoning mental crookedness
                • uju: not showing the virtues that one does not have (asaṭha) suhuju: not consenting to gains accrued due to non-existent virtues
            • suvaco
              • One is easy to admonish (suvaco) when one does not show anger, displeasure, give excuses or starts criticizing another when being admonished, but listens respectfully, like Sāriputta Mahāthera. It is of two kinds as āmisahetusuvaco and dhammagāravahetusuvaco. The second is meant here
            • mudu
              • One is gentle (mudu) when one acts joyfully and kindly while performing physical and verbal actions, avoiding conflict and opposition, and cultivating harmony, being pleasant and welcoming like a safe harbour
            • anatimānī
              • One if free from superiority conceit (atimāna) due to birth, clan, and so on, like a caṇḍala boy, like a viper without fangs, like a bull without horns or like a floor mat
            • santussako
              • One is content (santussako) when possessed of the twelve types of santosa. Alternatively one is content with what is one's own (sakena tussako), with what is available (santena tussako) and content evenly (samena tussako)
            • subharo
              • One is easy to support (subharo) when one is content with what is offered being it little or much, and having made use of it happily, go about doing their own work
            • appakicco
              • One has few duties (appakicco) when one is not engaged in time consuming duties such as those in relation to building monasteries, managing Saṅgha properties, administrating novices and workers. One is free from the ten impediments:
                • "āvāso ca kulaṃ lābho, gaṇo kammañca pañcamaṃ, addhānaṃ ñāti ābādho, gantho iddhīti te dasāti"
            • sallahukavuttī
              • One has a light livelihood (sallahukavuttī) when one lives depending on few possessions, like a bird, such as the aṭṭhaparikkhāra:
                • "ticīvarañca pattañca vāsi suci ca bandhanaṁ parissāvanena aṭṭhete yuttayogassa bhikkhuno"
            • santindriyo
              • One has calm faculties (santindriyo or anuddhatindriyo) when one restrains lust and other defilements from arising when encountering pleasant or unpleasant objects
            • nipako
              • One is wise (nipako) when one is possessed of wisdom in protecting virtues, finding requisites, in the sattasappāya, or alternatively in the four sampajañña, namely, that of purpose, of suitability, of domain and of non-delusion
            • appagabbho
              • One is not impudent (appagabbho) when free of bodily, verbal and mental impudence such as disrespectful behavior towards teachers, in public places, or towards the Saṅgha.
            • kulesu ananugiddho
              • One is without attachment to families (kulesu ananugiddho) when one approaches suitable families drawing back body and mind, always as a newcomer, without attachment, like the moon that comes and goes without sorrowing with them (na sahasokī), and without rejoicing with them (na sahanandī)
            • na ca khuddamācare kiñci yena viññū pare upavadeyyuṁ
              • One should not perform even small misdeeds of body, speech or mind, for which one would experience the present danger (sandiṭṭhika ādīnava) of being censured by the wise. One should not disregard any evil as little, as it is said in Dhp 121:
                • "māvamaññetha pāpassa, na mantaṃ āgamissati, udabindunipātena, udakumbhopi pūrati, bālo pūrati pāpassa, thokaṃ thokampi ācinaṃ"
        • 2nd verse: "{{2210313097211969::santussako ca subharo ca, appakicco ca sallahukavutti; santindriyo ca nipako ca, appagabbho kulesvananugiddho.}}" "{{2210313097211969::Content, easy to support, with few duties, living lightly, have calm faculties, have mature wisdom, not beng impolite and being without greed for householders}}" #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • 3 santussako (content) #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • sakena tussako (one is satisfied with what is one’s own): related to the 4 nissaya (paṁsukūlacīvara, piṇḍapāta, rukkhamūlasesāsana and pūtimuttabhesajja)
            • santena tussako (one is satisfied with what is available)
            • samena tussako (one is evenly satisfied): one is neither attached to desirable objects nor aversed to undesirable ones but is content with all objects with a balanced mind or with intellectual equanimity
            • 4 ariyavaṁsa #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • cīvarasantosa
              • piṇḍapātasantosa
              • senāsanasantosa
              • pahānabhāvanāramatā (delight in the meditation of letting go)
              • note:
                • the first three should be practiced as follows:
                  • 1. a monk is content
                  • 2. he praises contentment
                  • 3. he does not engage in a wrong search (anesanā)
                  • 4. he is not agitated when he does not receive them
                  • 5. he makes use of them without infatuation, seeing the danger in them and understanding the escape from them
                  • 6. he does not extol himself or disparage others because of them
                • while for the fourth: a monk should not be content with a partial liberation and wholesome qualities; he should find delight in their development; he does not extol himself or disparage others based on this
          • subharo (one is easy to support)
            • vocab:
              • bharati↔supports, bears, maintains
            • 4 types of person according to bhara #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • attano dubbharo (one difficult to support by himself): one who is not satisfied with what is offered and keeps looking for something else, even to the point of coming back empty handed
                • yo hi ambilādīni laddhā anambilādīni pariyesati, aññassa ghare laddhaṃ aññassa ghare chaḍḍento sabbaṃ gāmaṃ vicaritvā rittapattova vihāraṃ pavisitvā nipajjati, ayaṃ attano dubbharo
              • upaṭṭhākānaṃ dubbharo (one difficult to be supported by others): one who shows displeasure at the donation and criticizes it
                • yo pana sālimaṃsodanādīnaṃ patte pūretvā dinnepi dummukhabhāvaṃ anattamanabhāvameva ca dasseti, tesaṃ vā sammukhāva taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ "kiṃ tumhehi dinna"nti apasādento, sāmaṇeragahaṭṭhādīnampi deti, ayaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ dubbharo
              • attano subharo (one easy to support by himself): one who is satisfied having received little or much
                • yo pana yaṃkiñci lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā laddhā tuṭṭhacittova bhuñjitvā vihāraṃ gantvā attano kammaṃ karoti, ayaṃ attano subharo
              • upaṭṭhākānaṃ subharo (one easy to be supported by others): one who is pleased with the donation and does not criticize it
                • yo ca paresampi appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā dānaṃ ahīḷetvā attamano vippasannamukho hutvā tesaṃ sammukhāva paribhuñjitvā yāti, ayaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ subharo.
          • appakicco (having few duties)
            • few duties may refer to one who has no duties in relation to building monasteries, Saṅgha properties, the administration of novices and monastery workers and so forth
            • 3 things lead to the decline of a trainee
              • delighting in work, talk, and sleep
            • āraññakasuttaṁ: one endowed with 5 factors attains the unshakeable in no long time:
              • idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu appaṭṭho hoti appakicco subharo susantoso jīvitaparikkhāresu, appāhāro hoti anodarikattaṃ anuyutto, appamiddho hoti jāgariyaṃ anuyutto, āraññako hoti pantasenāsano, yathāvimuttaṃ cittaṃ paccavekkhati
            • dasa paḷibodha gāthā (10 impediments) (Pop.III.29)
              • "āvāso ca kulaṃ lābho, gaṇo kammañca pañcamaṃ, addhānaṃ ñāti ābādho, gantho iddhīti te dasāti"
                • ñāti: kin (teacher, preceptor, co-residents...or mother, father....when they are sick)
                • gantho: books
                • iddhi: only an obstruction for insight, not for serenity; an obstruction for some individuals, not all
          • sallahukavutti (light livelihood)
              • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
          • santindriya (calm faculties)
            • one should restrain the faculties by not letting lust arise when experiencing pleasant objects and by restraining anger from arising when experiencing unpleasant objects
            • peaceful faculties are manifested when one has attained concentration, absorption, and enlightenment
            • King Pasenadi of Kosala, on dhammacetiyasuttaṁ: idha panāhaṃ, bhante, bhikkhū passāmi haṭṭhapahaṭṭhe udaggudagge abhiratarūpe pīṇindriye appossukke pannalome paradattavutte migabhūtena cetasā viharante
          • nipako (having mature wisdom, wise)
            • one is wise (nipako) wise in maintaining good behavior, in seeking robes and so forth, and with regard to the 7 kinds of suitability applied to
              • abodes,
              • alms resort,
              • speech,
              • companions,
              • food,
              • climate,
              • and posture
            • “sīle patiṭṭhāya {{8690825732264316::naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ; ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ}}.”
              • sapañño = jātipaññā↔understanding that is born of kamma by means of a rebirth-linking with triple rootcause
              • nepakkaṁ [nipaka + *ya] (nt.)↔skilfulness; astuteness; carefulness; circumspection; being adept
              • meaning of nipaka in vsm.I.3: nipakoti nepakkaṃ vuccati paññā, tāya samannāgatoti attho. iminā padena pārihārikapaññaṃ dasseti. imasmiñhi pañhābyākaraṇe tikkhattuṃ paññā āgatā. tattha paṭhamā jātipaññā, dutiyā vipassanāpaññā, tatiyā {{26165103618135865::sabbakiccapariṇāyikā pārihārikapaññā (protective understanding of all affairs or knowledge which is capable of carrying out any task to completion)}} which refers to the 4 sampajañña: #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • sātthakasampajañña (clear comprehension of purpose) #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • sappāyasampajañña (clear comprehension of suitability) #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • gocarasampajañña (clear comprehension of the domain) #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • asammohasampajañña (clear comprehension of reality) #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • note:
                  • meaning of nipaka in suttanta: nipaka = satinepakka = satisampajañña
            • vocab:
              • satinepakka [sati + nepakka] (nt.)→prudent mindfulness; careful awareness; (comm) mindfulness and prudence
              • parihārika (adj.) [pari + √har + *a + ika]↔looking after; taking care of (s.w/ p)
              • vijaṭayati [vi + √jaṭ + *aya + ti]↔pr. (+acc) untangles; unknots; untwists; unravels
              • jaṭā (f.) [√jaṭ + ā]↔dreadlocks; matted hair; 2 tangle; mess; snarl; knot
          • appagabbho (courteous, not impolite, not impudent)
            • 3 types of pagabbha:
              • kāyapagabbha (the eight cases of bodily impudence): modes of improper bodily behavior in regard to the Sangha, a group, an individual, in the refectory, in the sauna, at a ford for bathing, on the path to the alms round, and when entering among the houses.
              • vacīpagabbha (the four cases of verbal impudence): improper verbal utterances regarding the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, and among the houses.
              • manopagabbha (numerous cases of mental impudence): the various kinds of improper thoughts, such as thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of hatred and so on, pondered by the mind without falling into any kind of misconduct by way of body or speech
          • kulesu ananugiddho (without attachment to families)
            • one does not greeds after requisites of or forms inappropriate bonds with laypeople; he is neither sad nor happy with them; he is not anxious about their tasks and affairs; 3 similes from candūpamāsutta about how to approach families: "candūpamā, bhikkhave, kulāni upasaṅkamatha – apakasseva kāyaṃ, apakassa cittaṃ, niccanavakā kulesu appagabbhā #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • moon: when the moon rises in the sky, it is not attached to anyone, does not love or hate anyone and no one hates the moon because of that
              • jarudapānaṃ vā olokeyya pabbatavisamaṃ vā nadīviduggaṃ vā (old well / precipice / steep riverbank): a monk should draw back the body and mind and always act like a newcomer, without impudence towards families just as a man looking down an old well, a precipice, or a steep riverbank, would draw back the body and mind
              • ākāse pāṇi na sajjati na gayhati na bajjhati (hand in space): the Buddha moved his hand in the empty space and said that just as the hand is not stuck, held or caught in space, in the same way, when a monk approaches families, his mind should not be stuck, held or caught amidst families, thinking, “may those desiring gains obtain gains, may those desiring merits gain merits!” he is happy when others get something as if he himself had gotten it.
            • 5 drawbacks for a monk who visits families:
              • one falls into an offense for wandering without leave
              • one falls into an offense for sitting in a private place with a woman
              • one falls into an offense for sitting in a hidden place with a woman
              • one falls into an offense for teaching more than five or six sentences to a woman.
              • one has a lot of sensual thoughts
            • 5 drawbacks for a monk who approaches family for too long, mixing closely with lay people
              • he often sees a woman
              • when there is the seen, he becomes close
              • being close, one becomes intimate
              • being intimate, lust overcomes him
              • when his mind is overwhelmed by lust, it is to be expected that he will practice the holy life without satisfaction, or commit one of the corrupt offenses, or resign the training and return to a lower life
            • vocab:
              • ananugiddha adj. [na + anu + √gidh + ta]→(+loc) not greedy; without desire (among)
              • anugiddha↔pp. covetous, greedy (root: gidh)
              • giddha adj.↔(+loc) greedy (for); desirous (of); lit. greedy (root: gidh)
        • 3rd verse: "{{08802453096694118::na ca khuddamācare kiñci, yena viññū pare upavadeyyuṃ; sukhinova khemino hontu, sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā}}" "Let him not perform the slightest wrong for which wise men would censure him; (let him reflect thus:) ‘May all beings be happy and safe, may they have a pleased mind'" #[[khuddaka exam]]

            • Dhp 121: "māvamaññetha {{670536448104659::pāpassa, na mantaṃ āgamissati, udabindunipātena, udakumbhopi pūrati, bālo pūrati pāpassa, thokaṃ thokampi ācinaṃ}}" “do not disregard evil, thinking it will have no consequence, just as falling drops of water fill up a bucket, a fool becomes full of evil collecting it little by little.”
          • vocab:
            • avamaññati [ava + √man + ya + ti]↔pr. (+gen) thinks lightly (of); belittles; despises; lit. thinks down

            • ācinanta↔prp. (+acc) accumulating; gathering; collecting; heaping up

          • khema↔safe or without danger, and because of being safe from all dangers, one is peaceful
          • 1st method: sabbasaṅgahakamettā (loving-kindness including all beings); to be practiced after sīmāsambheda #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhino (may all beings be physically happy!)
            • sabbe sattā bhavantu khemino (may all beings be safe!)
            • sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all beings be mentally happy!)

"{{765532529404209::Those seen or not seen; those dwelling far or near; those born or those seeking rebirth – may all beings be happy}}" #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • diṭṭha: {{2234893664390496::those that have been previously seen when they came into the range of one’s own vision}} adiṭṭha: {{2234893664390496::those existing in places one has not seen}} #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • dūra: {{06494505836847853::those which are relatively far (outside one’s own body, the neighbourhood of one’s house, monastery, etc)}} avidūra: {{06494505836847853::those which are relatively close (within one’s own body, or within the neighbourhood of one’s house, monastery, village, district, continent and universe) }} #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • bhūta: {{25148705278270356::those that have come to be}} #[[khuddaka exam]] #[[review khuddaka]]
            • arahants who have come to be but will not come to be again
            • aṇḍajayoni (egg-born) after hatching
            • jalābujayoni (womb-born) after being born
            • saṁsedajayoni (moisture-born) and opapātikayoni (spontaneously-born) from the 2nd mind-moment onwards or after changing into another posture other than that they were born in
          • sambhavesī: {{52594086110095::those that will come to be}} #[[khuddaka exam]] #[[review khuddaka]]
            • puthujjanas and sekhas who have not abandoned the fetters of existence
            • aṇḍajayoni (egg-born) before hatching
            • jalābujayoni (womb-born) before being born
            • saṁsedajayoni (moisture-born) and opapātikayoni (spontaneously-born) on the 1st mind-moment or while keeping the same posture they were born in
          • catasso yoniyo – {{35816979954134576::aṇḍaja}}{{35816979954134576::yoni, }}{{35816979954134576::jalābuja}}{{35816979954134576::yoni, }}{{35816979954134576::saṃsedaja}}{{35816979954134576::yoni, }}{{35816979954134576::opapātika}}{{35816979954134576::yoni}}

          • 4 methods of dukamettā (pairs) #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi tasā vā thāvarā vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all living beings there are, that are shakeable or unshakeable, may they be happy)
            • ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi diṭṭhā vā adiṭṭhā vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all living beings there are, that are seen or unseen, may they be happy)
            • ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi dūre vā avidūre vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all living beings there are, that are far or near, may they have mental happiness)
            • ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi bhūtā vā sambhavesī vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all living beings there are, that have come to be or that will come to be, may they have mental happiness)
          • 3 methods of tikamettā (trios) #[[khuddaka exam]]
            • ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi dīghā vā rassakā vā majjhimā vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all living beings there are, that are long, short or medium, may they be happy)
            • ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi mahantā vā aṇukā vā majjhimā vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all living beings there are, that are big, minute or medium, may they be happy)
            • ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi thūlā vā aṇukā vā majjhimā vā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā (may all living beings there are, that are round, minute or medium, may they be happy)

    • ratanasuttaṁ
      • part I
        • background
          • infancy: the queen of Bārāṇasī, at the approach of dawn as it is the case of woman of merit, gave birth to a lump of flesh and had it bottled and cast into the Ganges; devas protected it and labeled it with vermillion in a golden leaf; a hermit found it and kept it in a clean place; after a fortnight there were two lumps and after another fortnight five protuberances formed and developed into head and limbs; one became a boy and the other a girl; the hermit became affectionate and milk came forth from his thumb; later he would give them the milk from the porridge; Licchavī: the babies were so skinless that whatever entered their bellies was all visible as if it was in a crystal jar; others say their skins were attached as if their skin were adhesive; for these reasons they were known as the Licchavīs (skinless or adhesive skin); growing up: the cowheards took up the responsibility over the babies and the hermit instructed them to marry them to each other, satisfy the king with the five products of a cow, receive a plot of land in return and there build a city and annoint the prince; Vajjī: due to being violent towards the other children they were considered as people to be avoided and the region became known as vajjī (from vajjetabba); Vesālī: when the prince was 16 he was annointed king in the new city and married to the girl and an agreement not to bring brides from outside nor send them out was made; 16 twins were born from their union; as the city grew three time it was extended and surrounded by walls 1 gāvuta apart; because of its repeated extension the city became known as Vesālī; during the Buddha's time Vesālī had 7707 royals, each with their own house, park, and so on; bhayas: a draught happened and due to it a famine; the poor died first and evil spirits came; because of the decay a plague broke out; thus Vesālī was overrun by three perils: famine, evil spirits, and plague; the king was investigated for misconduct but found innocent; they decided to invite the Buddha and sent 2 Licchavīs with gift to King Bimbisāra who sent them to the Buddha; being asked to go, the Buddha reflected that 100.000 koṭis of cakkavāḷas would be pervaded by the protective power of the Ratanasutta and that 84.000 beings would breakthrough to the Dhamma, and consented to go; travelling: King Bimbisāra prepared the road, built monasteries in each of the 5 yojanas until the Ganga and many more offerings, accompanying the Buddha with 500 disciples to the Ganga; the Licchavīs doubled the offerings; the Buddha crossed on a gem-studded seat; King Bimbisāra followed until the water was neck-deep; devas and nāgas made offerings; the banks were a yojana apart; the Licchavīs also went neck-deep to receive the Blesssed One; when He stepped his right foot on the bank the pokkharavassa started and cleaned the area; the Blessed One was escorted for 3 days, 1 yojana each day with double the offerings; Vesālī: reaching Vesālī, Sakka came and most evil spirits left; ven. Ānanda learned the Ratanasutta at the entrance of the city and followed the instructions of the Blessed One to walk around the 3 walls with the Licchavīs reciting the discourse with the items of ritual offerings; the venerable took water in the Buddha's bowl and sprinkled it around the city; remaining spirits fled; the plague subsided; people prepared the main hall for the Buddha; discourse: all gathered and the discourse was given by the Buddha; at the conclusion of which all disasters were quelled and 84.000 beings attained Nibbāna; some say the first 5 verses were preached by the Buddha while the remaining ones by ven. Ānanda; the last 3 verses were spoken by Sakka, The Buddha went on to teach the same for 7 days liberating 84.000 beings in each day, amounting to 588.000 nāgas and earth devas: after staying in Vesālī for two weeks, the Blessed One decided to leave; the princes honored him on the way back for 3 days again, and nāga kings made extravagant offerings, escorting the Buddha and 500 bhikkhus to the nāgas' abode where nāgas made offerings to which the Buddha spoke words of appreciation and left; earth deities also honored the Buddha with a grand display of parasols reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm returning to Rājagaha: He returned to Rājagaha, escorted by King Bimbisāra, with doubled offerings extending over five days explaining kamma and vipāka: in a casual conversation, the bhikkhus praised the Buddha for the miracles associated with his presence; The Buddha explained that these wonders were the result of a past act of generosity with spiritual power, and told the story of the brahmin Saṅkha and his son Susīma mem aid: infancy (Queen of Bārāṇasī, lump of flesh, Ganga, devas, hermit, boy/girl, thumb-milk, porridge) childhood (villagers, violent, vajjī, king, land) founding of Vesālī (marriage, 16 twins, 3 extensions, 1 gāvuta each, 7707) bhayas (dubbhikkha, amanussa, roga, investigating the kings, Buddha, convoy, 100.000 koṭis, 84.000 beings) journey (Bimbisāra's prep, 5 yojanas, gem-seat, devas and nāgas, pokkharavassa, x2 offerings, 3 yojanas) Vesālī (Sakka, Ānanda, procession, water, main hall, discourse, 84.000, 5/~/3, 7 days, 588.000) return to Rājagaha (2 weeks, 3 days to Gaṅga, nāga realm, parasols, Rājagaha, kammavipāka)
          • pokkharavassa↔red color rain that only wets those who wish to get wet
          • questions
            • why were they called “Licchavis”?
              • līnacchavitāya – because their skin was as if adhesive (the skin was very thin, the stomach and anything put into it looked like they were joined together, as if they had been sewn)
              • nicchavitāya – because they were as if skinless (whatever food entered the stomach of the children could be seen as if the stomachs were transparent)
              • mem aid: li ⇒ līna ⇒ ni
              • vocab:
                • chavi (f.)↔skin; outer skin
                • līna↔adj. sluggish; dull; stuck
            • why was the region extending for 300 yojanas all around called 'Vajjī'?
              • the term "Vajjī" is derived from the act of avoiding or shunning those children (vajjetabbā ime) because of their violent behavior towards other children and the term was later used to refer to the region associated with this event
            • how was the city of Vesālī originated?
              • when the 16 y.o. Licchavi boy married his Licchavī sister and was annointed king, they gave birth to twins from their very first union – a daughter and a son; this happened a total of 16 times, resulting in sixteen sets of twins (32); as they grew up, the city became too small and people had to build walls around the city three times extending its territory. Each time they added a bit more space to the city by extending the walls a distance of a gāvuta (half a yojana). The city got the name Vesāli since it was enlarged several times (tassa punappunaṃ visālīkatattā vesālītveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ).
            • how prosperous was Vesālī during the Buddha’s time?
              • Vesāli was large and prosperous. It had 7,707 royals who were involved in governing. A similar number of princes, generals, treasurers, mansions, parks and lotus ponds were also there
            • what perils (bhaya) befell Vesāli?
              • dubbhikkha bhaya
              • amanussa bhaya
              • roga bhaya

            • 6 different meanings of ratana and gāthā
              • cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ (the gem in the sense of being honored): before the arising of the Buddha, people showed honor and venerated the cakka and maṇi ratana; after His appearance these ratana's power decline, the wheel gets dislocated from its proper position, the rāja sees signs of his impending death (there cannot be cajjavattirāja at the same time as a Sammāsambuddha in the world so the rāja either ordains or passes away); so since His appearance beings worship only Him

                • confirm if there can be a cakkavattirāja at the same time as a sammāsambuddha #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • mahagghaṭṭhena ratanaṃ (the gem in the sense of being of great value): cloth from Kāsī is considered very valuable and the Buddha mentioned that even when old, it has a pleasant appearance, touch and is of great value; but beings are valued according to the extent to which the donations made to them bear fruit (dakkhiṇeyya puggala) and whoever offers cloths to the Buddha, gets results of greater value than kāsī cloth
              • atulaṭṭhena ratanaṃ (the gem in the sense of being incomparable): the 7 treasures of a cakkavattirāja with all their great qualities are not comparable to the glory of the Bhagavā's qualities which are without comparison; these are the 7 treasures of a cakkavattirāja:
                • cakkaratana (the wheel-gem)
                  • it has 1.000 spokes made of 7 gems; a hub made of sapphire, a rim made of coral, a linchpin of gold; every 10 spokes 1 special one catches the wind and produces a sweet sound; on each side of the hub there is a lion mouth; it is made of kammapaccayautujarūpa; its sound can be heard 12 yojanas away and its form seen a yojana away; it appears as a rising moon to a righteous King on the uposatha day while he is observing precepts; he sprinkles it with water and it goes east and is followed by the monarch with his army; other kings submit without a fight and the monarch gives them the 5 precepts; the wheel plunges into the eastern ocean and emerges again heading towards the south...west...north...returns to the capital and remains as if fixed on its axle at the gate of the monarch's inner palace
                • hatthiratana (the elephant-gem)
                  • it is all white, has supernormal powers, is able to fly, belongs to either the highest ranking of the Uposatha clan or the lowest of the Chaddanta clan; he can trasverse the whole earth leaving in the morning and coming back for breakfast
                  • 10 types of elephants mentioned in the Theravada literature: kālavaka, gaṅgeyya, paṇḍara, tamba, piṅgala, gandhahatthi, maṅgala, hemavata, uposatha and chaddanta
                • assaratana (the horse-gem)
                  • it is all white with red feet, with black head, the mane like muñja grass and belongs to the Sindhava clan; it is called valāhaka since it can fly
                • maṇiratana (the jewel-gem)
                  • it is eight-faceted, comes from mount Vepulla, its radience shines for a whole yojana making it look as if it was day-time
                • itthiratana (the woman-gem)
                  • she surpasses human beauty without reaching divine beauty; she is never unfaithful; she is either the original chief queen of the monarch or comes from Uttarakuru or from the Madda royal family
                • gahapatiratana (the steward-gem)
                  • a treasurer with the divine-eye who can see stores of treasures for a yojana' when testing him the monarch asks for gold in the middle of the Ganga and he pulls from the water a pot full of gold;
                • pariṇāyakaratana (the commander-gem or the counsellor-gem)
                  • wise consellor which promotes what is right; he is the monarch's eldest son; when the cakkaratana appears he becomes capable of reading other's minds to the distance of 12 yojanas
              • dullabhadassanaṭṭhena ratanaṃ (the gem in the sense of being rarely seen): a wheel turning monarch is rare in the world, with only a few appearing every antarakappa but a sammāsambuddha is much more rare; due to that the deities complained they could not see the Buddha on his final moments because ven. Upavāna was standing in front and he was an arahant

              • ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ (the gem in the sense of producing delight): the wheel gem of a wheel-turning monarch can create various indescribable things which produce abundant delight for the king but that delight is not worth a sixteenth part of celestial delight and yet, the delight of all absorptions, paths and fruitions arising due to the Tathāgata are more excellent and sublime than celestial delight

          • various classifications of gems #editing
            • 11.1.Aviññāṇaka (insentient or inanimate) ratana is the wheel gem, the jewel gem, gold, silver, diamond or anything else devoid of faculties born out of kamma. On the other hand, saviññāṇaka (sentient or animate) ratana is the hatthi ratana, pariṇāyaka ratana, gahapati ratana, or anything else endowed with sense faculties. Among these two, the sentient gem is superior since insentient gems are used to adorn the sentient, such as the elephant gem.
            • 11.2.Saviññāṇaka (sentient) ratana is also of two kinds: Tiracchānagataratana (animal gems) and manussa-ratana (human gems). The later one is superior because the animal gems are used as conveyances or vehicles for human gems.
            • 11.3.Manussa ratana (human gems) is also of two kinds: Itthiratana (female gems) and purisaratana (male gems). The later one is superior since female gems provide service to male gem.
            • 11.4.Purisa ratana (male gems) is also of two kinds: Agārika ratana (home dwelling gems) and Anagārika ratana (homeless gems). The later one is superior since even the wheel-turning monarch, kings and so forth pay homage to homeless gems who possess excellent qualities such as good behavior, etc., attend on them and by that they achieve celestial and human prosperity and the Nibbāna.
            • 11.5.Anagārika ratana (homeless gems) is also of two kinds: Puthujjana ratana (worldling gems) and Ariya ratana (noble gems). Out of the two, ariya ratana is superior to puthujjana ratana.
            • 11.6.Ariya ratana (the gem of the noble ones), too, is of two kinds: Sekha-ratana (trainee gems) and Asekha-ratana (adept, arahant, one who does not require any further training).
            • 11.7.Asekha ratanam (the gem of Arahant), too, is of two kinds: Sukkavipassaka (dry-insight arahants) and Samathayānika (those who use serenity as their vehicle). Out of the two, Samathayānika ratana is superior to Sukkavipassaka ratana.
            • 11.8.Samathayānika ratana (those who use serenity as their vehicle) is also of two kinds: Sāvakapāramippatta (those who have reached the perfection of a disciple) and Sāvakapāramī-appatta (those who have not reached it). The first one is superior because of the greatness of their excellent qualities.
            • 11.9.The gem of a Paccekabuddha is declared superior to one who has reached the perfection of a disciple. Why? because of the greatness of his excellent qualities. For many hundred disciples like the Venerable Sāriputta and Moggallāna are not equal to a hundredth portion of the excellent qualities of a single Paccekabuddha.
            • 11.10.The gem of Sammāsambuddha is declared superior to a Paccekabuddha. Why? Because of the greatness of his excellent qualities. For if Paccekabuddhas sitting cross-legged next to one another were to fill all Jambudīpa, they would not amount to a sixteenth part or a portion of a sixteenth part of the excellent qualities of a single fully enlightened Buddha. And this was said by the Blessed One: Bhikkhus, “To whatever extent there are beings, whether footless or with two feet, four feet, or many feet, whether having form or formless, whether percipient or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient, the 29 Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is declared the foremost among them.”8 In this way, too, there is no gem equal to the Tathāgata. Hence the Blessed One says: “There is none equal to the Tathāgata.

          • Sugatassa sāvakā (the disciple of the Sugata)
            • the Buddha is called Sugata (The Well-Gone One) because:
              • 19.1. Because he is endowed with a beautiful manner of going (sobhanena gamanena yuttattā): The Buddha has gone on the Noble eightfold path in a manner that is good, purified and blameless, and has thus gone without attachment in the direction of safety, namely the Nibbāna. (eightfold noble path)
              • 19.2. Because he has gone to the beautiful excellent place (sobhanaṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā): Since the Buddha has gone to the beautiful excellent state called the Nibbāna, he is called Sugata. (Nibbāna)
              • 19.3. Because he has gone well (suṭṭhu gatattā): The Buddha has gone well without going back to the defilements abandoned by each supramundane path.
              • 19.4. Because of enunciating well (suṭṭhu gadattā): The Buddha speaks appropriately at the right time and place.
            • Sāvaka means those who listen to the Buddha’s words and attain the paths and fruitions, or in other words, disciples.
          • Etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni (gifts given to the disciples of the Buddha yield abundant fruit): Even small donations given to the disciples of the Buddha produces abundant results because of the purification of the offerings through the recipient.
            • There are four purifications of offerings or gifts (dakkhiṇā visuddhi):
              • 20.1.1. The offering purified on the part of the giver, not the recipient (dakkhiṇā dāyakato visujjhati no paṭiggāhakato).
              • 20.1.2. The offering purified on the part of the recipient, not the giver (dakkhiṇā paṭiggāhakato visujjhati no dāyakato).
              • 20.1.3. The offering purified on neither side (dakkhiṇā neva dāyakato visujjhati no paṭiggāhakato).
              • 20.1.4. The offering purified on both sides (dakkhiṇā dāyakato ceva visujjhati paṭiggāhakato ca).
            • Hence, in another Sutta, it is said: To whatever extent there are Saṅghas or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence 40 in the foremost, and for those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.2
            • a gift from the buddha to sāriputta is higher than from sāriputta to the buddha; purity of the donor is more influential than the purity of the recipient

          • "Kiñcāpi so kammaṃ karoti pāpakaṃ, kāyena vācā uda cetasā vā, abhabho so tassa paṭicchadāya, abhabbatā diṭṭhapadassa vuttā, Idampi saṅghe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, etena saccena suvatthi hotu” Although one does a bad deed by body, speech, or mind, one is incapable of concealing it; such inability is stated for one who has seen the state. This too is the sublime gem in the Sangha: by this truth, may there be safety!
          • vocab:
            • kiñcāpi↔although, even though
            • abhabbatā↔such inability
            • diṭṭhapadassa↔for one who has seen the state
          • purpose→to express that he is also incapable of concealing even trifling bad deeds that he may have done
          • sotāpannas do not intentionally breach any rules promulgated by the Buddha but due to lack of mindfulness they might unknowingly committ paññattivajja offenses; here classified according to kammadvāra
            • kāyena pāpakaṃ kammaṃ karoti (bad deed by body)
              • building a kuṭi contrary to regulations (kuṭikāraka sikkhāpada)
              • sleeping together with a novice more than three days (sahaseyya sikkhāpada), etc.
            • vācā(ya) pāpakaṃ kammaṃ karoti (bad deed by speech)

                • padasodhamma sikkhāpada: making a non-upasampadā person recite the Dhamma together with him

              • by anupasampanna
                • pharusavācā
                • samphappalāpa

              • giving an opportunity for greed or hatred to arise sometimes
              • unknowingly accepting jātarūparajata
              • forgetting to reflect on the use of the four requisites and so on
            • note:
              • the Buddha says he may fall into offenses in regard to lesser and minor (khuddānukhuddaka - non-prjk) training rules but not those that are fundamental to the noble life (prjk)
                • ime pana aṅguttaramahānikāyavaḷañjanaka-ācariyā ‘cattāri pārājikāni ṭhapetvā sesāni sabbānipi khuddānukhuddakāni' - the teachers who specialize in the Great Aṅguttara Nikāya say, ‘Apart from the four pārājikas (offenses entailing expulsion), all the rest are lesser and minor'
                • ādibrahmacariyikānī ti maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtāni cattāri mahāsīlasikkhāpadāni; brahmacariyasāruppānī ti tāni yeva catumaggabrahmacariyassa sāruppāni anucchavikāni Those training rules that are fundamental to the spiritual life: these are the four major training rules fundamental to the spiritual life of the path. In conformity with the spiritual life: these same [rules] are in conformity with, fitting for, the spiritual life of the four paths
          • abhabbo so tassa paṭicchadāya (even if he commits those bad deeds, he is incapable of concealing them): Immediately, he discloses them to the teacher, wise fellow monks and corrects it in accordance with the Dhamma and restrains himself in the future.
          • abhabbatā diṭṭhapadassa vuttā (such inability is stated of one who has seen Nibbāna)
            • "bhikkhus, just as a young, tender infant lying prone at once draws back when he puts his hand or foot on a live coal, so too, this is the character of a person who possesses right view: although he may commit some kind of offense for which a means of rehabilitation has been laid down, still he at once confesses, reveals, and discloses it to the Teacher or wise fellow monks, and then enters upon restraint for the future"
        • 12th verse #edited
          • “Vanappagumbe yathā phussitagge, gimhānamāse paṭhamasmiṃ gimhe, tathūpamaṃ dhammavaraṃ adesayi, nibbānagāmiṃ paramaṃ hitāya, idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, etena saccena suvatthi hotu" Like a woodland thicket with flowering crests in a summer month, in the first (month) of the summer, just so the excellent Dhamma preached (scriptures), leading to nibbāna, for the supreme welfare (of beings). This too is the sublime gem in the Buddha: by this truth, may there be safety!
          • vocab:

            • phussita [√phus + ya + ita]↔adj. flowering; in full blossom; lit. flowered
            • gimhānamāse paṭhamasmiṃ gimhe↔in the first month of the summer, called Citta, aka the youthful spring (bālavasanta)
              • Paṭhamasmiṃ gimhe, citramāse ti attho. So hi paṭhamagimho ti ca bālavasanto ti ca vuccati It may sound contradictory to call this season both “summer” and “spring,” but in northern India the year is divided into three major seasons: the hot season, from mid-March until mid-July; the rainy season, from mid-July until mid-November; and the cool season, from mid-November until mid-March. The early part of the hot season would be called spring, and the later part summer. The month of Cittaruns from mid-March until mid-April, followed by Visākhā, from mid-April to mid-May, the month in which the Theravāda tradition celebrates the Buddha’s birth, enlightenment, and parinibbāna
                • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
            • tathūpamaṃ↔just so (tathā upamaṃ)

            • dhammavaraṃ↔the excellent Dhamma
            • adesayi↔taught, expounded
          • purpose→to express the truth found on the Buddha based on the scriptural Dhamma

                • (3) paññādhiṭṭhāna paripūraṇato: The Buddha is the “knower of the excellent” by the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom

            • varado (giver of the excellent); the Buddha is called so because

          • "Yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatāni, bhummāni vā yāni vā antalikkhe, Tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, buddhaṃ...dhammaṃ...saṅghaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotu" Whatever beings are gathered here, whether of the earth or in the sky, we pay homage to the thus-gone Buddha...Dhamma...Saṅgha venerated by devas and humans: may there be safety!
          • purpose→to express the Triple Tathāgatas (uttered by Sakka)
          • Triple Tathāgata
            • Tathāgataṃ Buddhaṃ; He is so called because
              • Tathā āgatoti tathāgato: The Buddha is called the Tathāgata, because he has come thus, in the way those zealous for the welfare of the world should come
              • Tathā gatoti tathāgato: The Buddha is called the Tathāgata, because he has gone thus, in the way those zealous for the welfare of the world should go
              • Tathā ājānatoti tathāgato: The Buddha is called the Tathāgata, because he has understood in the way those zealous for the welfare of the world should understand
              • The Buddha is called the Tathāgata, because he has known in the way those zealous for the welfare of the world should know
              • The Buddha is called the Tathāgata, because his utterances are in the way those zealous for the welfare of the world should utter
            • Tathāgataṃ Dhammaṃ; the Dhamma is called so because
              • the lokuttaramagga has gone to the group of defilements (kilesapakkha) eradicating them with the help of the power of samatha and vipassanā
              • Nibbāna is called Tathāgata since it is realized (avagata) by the beings such as the Buddhas in a way that all suffering is eradicated
            • Tathāgataṃ Saṅghaṃ; the Saṅgha is called so because
              • It has gone along each path in the way that those practicing for their own welfare must go

        • summary of the story of Brahmin Saṅkha and his son, Susīma
          • Brahmin Saṅkha's son, Susīma, seeks to learn a craft in Bārāṇasī. Susīma learns in a few months what normally took 12 years, but seeks the craft's end, which his teacher doesn't know, referring him to the Paccekabuddhas. He goes to Isipatana to ask paccekabuddhas, who ordain him and teach him conduct. Susīma attains pacceka enlightenment, attains to gain and renown but has a short life. His father, Saṅkha, seeks him in Bārāṇasī and learns about Susīma's enlightenment and passing. Saṅkha grieves and makes pūjā at Susīma's cetiya. The Blessed One connects the story with the present, revealing he was Saṅkha. The act of generosity in the past leads to grand offerings. The Dhamma talk concludes with a verse on renouncing slight happiness for greater happiness. merits done by Saṅkha at Susīma's cetiya and the kammic results they produced in the context of ratanasutta: 1. he plucked out the weeds: as a consequence the stumps and thorns along the eight-yojana journey were removed and the ground was made smooth and clean 2. he brought sand in his upper garment and scattered it over the terrace: as a consequence sand was scattered over the eight-yojana journey 3. he made an offering of woodland flowers: as a consequence, over the nine-yojana journey including land and water, a carpet was made with various flowers 4. he moistened the ground with water from his pot: as a consequence, a lotus-leaf rain fell on Vesālī 5. he set up a banner and tied a parasol there: as a consequence, banners were set up and row upon row of parasols were raised aloft right up to the Akaniṭṭha heaven verse: "mattāsukhapariccāgā, passe ce vipulaṃ sukhaṃ, caje mattāsukhaṃ dhīro, sampassaṃ vipulaṃ sukhaṃ“ If by renouncing a slight happiness one sees a greater happiness ahead, the wise person should give up the slight happiness, considering the greater happiness ahead (Dhp 290) Summary: A Brahmin's son, Susīma, seeks knowledge in Bārāṇasī, attains enlightenment as a paccekabuddha, and his father, Saṅkha, later learns of his son's fate, makes pūjās at his cetiya (weeds, sand, flowers, water, banner and parasol), The Buddha explains He was Saṅkha and shows the results of the meritorious deeds ending with a verse

      • sampajānakatadāna↔dāna accompanied by understanding about kamma and vipāka
        • dānañca dānaphalañca / kammañca kammaphalañca saddahitvā
        • faith purifies the mind (basic function) udakapasādamaṇi; when the mind is purified by faith it can accept objects more easily like pure water reflects images (secondary function)
        • wisdom on the other hand help seeing deep realities
        • only when saddhā is associating wisdom, has the mind the capacity to accept deep realities
        • if wisdom is missing only saddhā cannot accept deep realities
        • if someone believes in Buddha, kamma and vipāka, it must be with a mind of saddhā accompanied by wisdom
      • dāna goes agains a few kilesas
        • dāna is not opposite of rāga in terms of ujupaṭipaka, but to some tipes of lobha related to keeping things to oneself, to possessing things, to being rich, and to some extent sakkāyadiṭṭhi (because of the self view we tend to keep things to ourselves)
        • dāna's ujupaṭipakka is certain types of lobha
        • ujupaṭipakka: direct enemy (complete opposite)
        • rāga's ujupaṭipakka is asubha; metta's is dosa
        • some attributes of sotāpanna: muttacāgī, bhayatthapānī
        • no stinginess does not mean one gives everything away: upalavaṇṇa did not give her robe when asked since it is difficult to find robes
